lessons.title: Recursive contracts and progress
lessons.summary: State a domain, a base case and a measure that cannot decrease forever.
lessons.body:
A function is **recursive** when its execution can call itself, directly or through other functions. To make a terminating recursive algorithm, use a well-founded progress measure: it can never decrease forever (no infinite decreasing chain). A common design has these two properties:

1. There is at least one **base case**: an input small enough to answer directly, with no further calls.
2. Every recursive call makes **progress** towards a base case.

Recursion is the foundation for the rest of this module. Divide and conquer, backtracking and (in a later module) dynamic programming are all recursive ways of thinking, even when the final code uses a loop.

## The shape of a recursive function

Summing the digits of a non-negative integer is a small example. The numerical functions below validate that domain; trees are assumed finite and acyclic.

```python
def digit_sum(n):
    # Reject inputs outside the stated
    # domain.
    if type(n) is not int or n < 0:
        raise ValueError("nonnegative n")
    if n < 10:              # base case
        return n
    # recursive case: last digit plus the
    # digit sum of everything before it
    return n % 10 + digit_sum(n // 10)

print(digit_sum(4096))      # 19
```

Each call strips one digit, so the input shrinks and must eventually fall below 10. That is the progress guarantee.

Almost every recursive function follows the same recipe:

- **Identify the smallest inputs** (empty list, 0, a leaf node, a single character) and answer them directly.
- **Assume the function already works** for anything smaller than the current input.
- **Combine** that smaller answer with a little local work to answer the current input.

## The leap of faith

The second step is the one beginners resist. When you write `digit_sum(n // 10)`, you should *not* try to trace every call in your head. Instead, trust that it returns the right digit sum for the shorter number, and only check that your combining step is correct.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: asking the row in front
> In a dark cinema you want to know your row number. You can't count the rows, so you ask the person in front. They ask the person in front of them, and so on, until someone in the front row answers "row 1". Each person then adds one to the answer they receive and passes it back.
>
> **How it maps:** each person is one recursive call. The front row is the base case, answered directly. Asking the person in front is the recursive call on a smaller input, and "add one" is the combining step. Nobody needs to know how the person in front got their answer: that is the leap of faith.
>
> **Where it stops:** people in a cinema eventually reach the front row without anyone checking. A program has no such guarantee: you must prove that every call moves towards a base case, and every pending call uses memory until the answers come back.

This is exactly **proof by induction**:

| Induction | Recursion |
|---|---|
| Base case holds | Base case returns correctly |
| Assume true for k | Trust the smaller call |
| Prove for k + 1 | Combine into the answer |

Thinking this way scales. To count nodes in a binary tree, you say: an empty tree has 0 nodes; otherwise it has 1 plus the count of the left subtree plus the count of the right subtree. The correctness argument need not trace every depth; resource usage still depends on the height.

```python
def count(node):
    # An empty subtree contributes no nodes.
    if node is None:
        return 0
    # Combine the two smaller subtree
    # answers.
    return 1 + count(node.left) \
             + count(node.right)
```

> [!tip] Define the function's contract first
> Write one sentence: "`count(node)` returns the number of nodes in the subtree rooted at `node`." The leap of faith is only safe if the contract is precise and every call respects it.

## Common pitfalls

- **Missing base case, or one that is never reached.** `fact(-1)` with base case `n == 0` recurses forever (until `RecursionError`). Reject negative input: changing the base case to `n <= 1` alone terminates but incorrectly returns 1 for negative factorials.
- **Not shrinking the input.** Calling `f(n)` from `f(n)` with a different flag still needs a measure that strictly decreases.
- **Repeated subproblems.** Exponential blow-up, as with naive `fib`.
- **Expensive arguments.** For a copied slice of length n, slicing lists or strings per call adds hidden O(n) work.
- **Shared mutable state.** Appending to one list across calls is fine, but remember every frame sees the same object (this matters a lot in backtracking).

## Key takeaways
- State a domain, a base case and a measure that cannot decrease forever.
- Trust smaller calls only after establishing their contract and progress.

## Further reading
- [Recursive algorithms — Erickson](https://jeffe.cs.illinois.edu/teaching/algorithms/book/01-recursion.pdf)
- [Recursion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recursion_(computer_science))

lessons.title: Reading the call stack
lessons.summary: Pending work resumes after a recursive call returns.
lessons.body:
## What the call stack actually does

The leap of faith is how you *design* recursion. To *debug* it, and to understand its cost, you need the machine's view.

Conceptually, a pending call has a **stack frame** holding parameters, local state and where execution resumes. Implementations can inline calls or eliminate tail calls; the examples here use ordinary CPython frames. A returned frame may remain referenced by debugging or traceback objects. Here is `fact(3)` at its deepest point:

```python
def fact(n):
    # Reject inputs outside the stated
    # domain.
    if type(n) is not int or n < 0:
        raise ValueError("nonnegative n")
    if n <= 1:
        return 1
    # Keep this multiplication pending on
    # return.
    return n * fact(n - 1)
```

```
 top   fact(1)  returns 1
       fact(2)  waiting: 2 * ?
       fact(3)  waiting: 3 * ?
 base  <module>
```

Then the stack unwinds: `fact(1)` returns 1, `fact(2)` computes 2 × 1 = 2, `fact(3)` computes 3 × 2 = 6.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: a pile of paused tasks
> You are filling in a form when a question sends you to look something up in a second document, which in turn refers you to a third. Each time, you leave a sticky note on the page you were working on saying what you still have to do there. When the third lookup is finished you return to the most recent note first, then the one below it.
>
> **How it maps:** each sticky note is a stack frame: it records where to resume and what is still pending, such as "multiply by 3". The pile is the call stack; the newest note is always dealt with first, which is why work after a recursive call runs on the way back up.
>
> **Where it stops:** a desk can hold as many notes as you like. A real call stack has a fixed allowance (CPython's recursion limit) and each frame costs memory, so a very deep pile fails rather than just getting taller.

Two consequences follow:

- **Space is proportional to depth.** With constant-sized frame state, a recursion that is d calls deep at its deepest point costs O(d) control-stack space: d frames, each of fixed size. Retained lists, arbitrary-size integers and other objects must be counted separately. A recursive function over a linked list of length n uses O(n) space; over a balanced tree of n nodes, O(log n).
- **Work after the call happens on the way back up.** Along a single call chain, code before the call runs on descent and code after it runs on return; multiple recursive branches are completed in the order the code calls them.

```python
def show(n):
    # Reject inputs outside the stated
    # domain.
    if type(n) is not int or n < 0:
        raise ValueError("nonnegative n")
    if n == 0:
        return
    print(n, end=" ")    # on the way down
    # Pause this frame until the smaller
    # call ends.
    show(n - 1)
    print(n, end=" ")    # on the way up

show(3)   # 3 2 1 1 2 3
```

### Python's recursion limit

CPython limits active recursion and raises `RecursionError` when the configured allowance is exhausted. The usual default is **1000**; inspect `sys.getrecursionlimit()` rather than assuming how many calls remain. Since CPython 3.11, most Python-to-Python calls no longer consume C stack per call. Raising the limit still increases memory/resource exposure, and calls involving C code can have separate stack limits; the documentation warns that an excessively high setting can crash the process.

In practice: a million-node binary tree with near-minimum height has about 20 levels, well below the usual recursion allowance when entered from a shallow call stack. Recursion over a list, a string, or a tree that might degenerate into a chain is a bug waiting for large input.

## Key takeaways
- Pending work resumes after a recursive call returns.
- Control-stack space depends on maximum nesting, not on the number of nodes visited.

## Further reading
- [Python recursion allowance](https://docs.python.org/3/library/sys.html)
- [CPython 3.11 call changes](https://docs.python.org/3/whatsnew/3.11.html)

questions.prompt: A recursive `height(node)` function on a binary search tree uses `1 + max(height(left), height(right))`. The tree holds 1,000,000 keys. What is its worst-case **stack** usage if the tree is (a) of minimum possible height, (b) built by inserting keys in sorted order without rebalancing?

options.text: (a) O(log n), about 20 frames; (b) O(n), about 1,000,000 frames
options.explanation: Correct. With n the number of keys, stack usage equals the maximum recursion depth, which is the tree height: twenty non-null node levels at minimum height, and n when sorted inserts produce a chain.

options.text: (a) O(n); (b) O(n), because every node is visited
options.explanation: This confuses time with space. Every node is visited (O(n) time), but frames are popped as each subtree finishes, so only one root-to-leaf path is on the stack at once.

options.text: (a) O(1); (b) O(1), because `max` is called after both results return
options.explanation: Each pending call still holds a frame while its child calls run. The depth of nesting, not the order of operations, determines stack usage.

options.text: (a) O(log n); (b) O(log n), because BSTs are always logarithmic
options.explanation: A plain BST has no balancing. Inserting sorted keys puts every new key in the right child of the last, forming a chain of n nodes and n − 1 edges.

questions.workedExample:
1. **Space follows the maximum depth of pending calls**, which for a tree recursion is the tree height, not the number of nodes. Frames for a finished subtree are popped before the next subtree starts.
2. **Minimum height:** each extra level can hold twice as many nodes as the one above, so a million keys fit in about 20 levels (2 to the power 20 is just over a million). About twenty non-null frames are pending at once; a conventional null-base-case traversal adds one terminal null frame.
3. **Sorted inserts into an unbalanced BST:** keys 1 → 2 → 3 → ... each become a right child, forming a chain. All 1,000,000 non-null nodes lie on one path (999,999 edges), so a million frames are pending at the deepest point, plus the terminal null call.
4. In CPython, (b) raises RecursionError long before finishing; in C it can exhaust the native stack, whose allowance depends on the process, thread and operating system.

Lesson: logarithmic depth is often manageable, but safety still depends on available stack and per-frame resources. When depth depends on data shape, prefer an explicit stack.

lessons.title: Repeated calls and hidden slice costs
lessons.summary: A recursion tree counts repeated work, not just distinct arguments.
lessons.body:
## The cost of recursion: recursion trees

When a function makes more than one recursive call, draw the **recursion tree** to estimate its cost. Each non-base invocation of naive Fibonacci makes two recursive calls:

```python
def fib(n):
    # Reject inputs outside the stated
    # domain.
    if type(n) is not int or n < 0:
        raise ValueError("nonnegative n")
    if n < 2:
        return n
    # The two branches repeat smaller
    # arguments.
    return fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2)
```

```
            fib(4)
          /        \
      fib(3)       fib(2)
      /    \       /    \
  fib(2) fib(1) fib(1) fib(0)
  /    \
fib(1) fib(0)
```

Count the boxes: `fib(4)` makes 9 calls, `fib(5)` makes 15 and `fib(30)` makes about 2.7 million, yet there are only n + 1 different arguments (0 to n). The same subproblems are solved again and again: `fib(2)` appears twice in the small tree above, and far more often in bigger ones.

The call count itself follows a Fibonacci-like pattern, because each call is one call plus all the calls its two children make. So each step up in the argument multiplies the number of calls by roughly 1.6 (the golden ratio): exponential growth.

```formula reference
C(n) = 1 + C(n − 1) + C(n − 2)
C(n) = 2F(n + 1) − 1
where
C(n): the total number of calls that fib(n) makes, including itself, for n of at least 2; C(0) = C(1) = 1
n: the non-negative whole number passed to fib
F(n): the nth Fibonacci number (F(0) = 0, F(1) = 1, each later one the sum of the previous two)
In words: a call is itself plus the calls of its two children, which makes the call count about twice a Fibonacci number, growing by a factor of about 1.6 per step.
```

Caching results (memoisation) removes the repetition: each argument is computed once, so the number of additions drops to O(n). The integers still get longer as n grows, so this is not an O(n) bit-cost claim. That idea is the heart of the dynamic programming module.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: a family tree of questions
> Imagine a family-history volunteer who, asked about a person, must separately research both parents, and for each parent research both of theirs, without keeping notes. When distant cousins have married, the same people appear on several branches and get researched again every time they turn up.
>
> **How it maps:** each research job is a call; the two parents are the two recursive calls; a person who appears on several branches is a repeated subproblem such as `fib(2)`. Keeping a notebook of finished answers is memoisation.
>
> **Where it stops:** in a real family tree, people shared between branches turn up irregularly and the records eventually run out. Naive Fibonacci repeats in a perfectly regular way and always ends at the base cases 0 and 1, which is what makes its call count follow its own Fibonacci pattern.

## Hidden O(n) work per call

Here n is the original list length. `return xs[0] + total(xs[1:])` looks linear, but each slice copies the rest of the list:

- The first call copies n − 1 references, the next n − 2, and so on down to 0. Those copies add up to about half of n squared, so the running time is **O(n²)**, assuming constant-cost element addition.
- Every frame keeps its slice alive until it returns, and at the deepest point all of the frames are still waiting. So peak memory is **O(n²)** as well, not just O(n) for the frames.

A thousand-item list makes about half a million reference copies instead of a thousand additions. The fix is to pass an index (`total(xs, i + 1)`) so each call does constant work, or, in Python, to use a loop.

## Key takeaways
- A recursion tree counts repeated work, not just distinct arguments.
- A copied slice retained by each frame can turn linear-looking recursion into quadratic work and storage.

## Further reading
- [Recursive cost analysis — Erickson](https://jeffe.cs.illinois.edu/teaching/algorithms/book/01-recursion.pdf)
- [Python lists and slices](https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/introduction.html#lists)

options.text: About 2.7 million plus one, because there is only one new argument
options.explanation: This counts distinct arguments, which is what memoisation would compute. Without a cache, fib(31) re-runs the whole fib(30) tree and the whole fib(29) tree as well.

options.text: About 5.4 million, because each call makes two calls
options.explanation: Doubling would be right if both children were as large as fib(30). The second child, fib(29), has a smaller tree, so the growth per step is less than 2.

options.text: About 4.4 million: roughly 1.6 times as many
options.explanation: Correct. fib(31) runs the fib(30) tree (about 2.7 million calls) plus the smaller fib(29) tree (about 1.7 million) plus itself. Each step multiplies the work by about the golden ratio, 1.6.

options.text: About 2.7 million, because the recursion depth only grows by one
options.explanation: Depth controls stack space, not the number of calls. The tree grows in width at every level, so the total grows much faster than the depth.

questions.workedExample:
1. A call is itself plus all the calls its two children make: fib(31) = one call + the fib(30) tree + the fib(29) tree.
2. The fib(30) tree has about 2.7 million calls and the fib(29) tree about 1.7 million, so fib(31) makes about 4.4 million.
3. The ratio between consecutive call counts settles near 1.6, the golden ratio, because the call counts follow a Fibonacci-like pattern themselves.
4. Small check: fib(4) makes 9 calls and fib(5) makes 15 (one plus 9 plus 5), also about 1.6 times as many.

The arguments 0 to 31 are only 32 distinct subproblems; memoising them would make about 32 distinct computations instead of millions of calls.

options.text: Θ(n) time and Θ(n) peak memory
options.explanation: This counts only the n calls and n frames (n is the list length). It misses that `xs[1:]` copies the remaining list on every call.

options.text: Θ(n²) time but only Θ(n) peak memory
options.explanation: The time is right, but each frame keeps its own slice alive until it returns. At the deepest point all n slices exist at once.

options.text: Θ(n²) time and Θ(n²) peak memory
options.explanation: Correct. For a list of n items, slicing copies n − 1, then n − 2, and so on, which adds up to about n²/2 copies. All those slices are still held by waiting frames at the deepest point, so peak memory is quadratic too.

options.text: Θ(n log n) time and Θ(log n) peak memory
options.explanation: This function removes one element per call, so there are n + 1 nested calls at the deepest point. Only halving the list on each call could give logarithmic depth.

questions.workedExample:
Here n is the length of the list, and Θ means "grows at exactly this rate, up to a constant factor".

1. There are n + 1 nested calls (one per element plus the empty-list base case).
2. Each call creates a fresh slice one element shorter than its own input: n − 1 references copied, then n − 2, and so on down to 0.
3. Those copies add up to about half of n squared, which dwarfs the n additions, so time is **Θ(n²)**.
4. Memory: when the deepest call runs, every earlier frame is still waiting to add `xs[0]`, and each holds a reference to its slice. The retained slices have lengths n − 1, n − 2, ... 1, again about n²/2 reference slots, so peak memory is **Θ(n²)**.
5. Fix: pass an index, `total(xs, i + 1)`, so each call does constant work and memory is O(n) frames. (And for n above about 1000 in Python, use a loop.)

lessons.title: Tail calls and accumulators
lessons.summary: A tail call returns its result without pending work.
lessons.body:
## Tail recursion

A call is a **tail call** if it is the very last thing a function does: its result is returned directly, with no work left to do afterwards.

- `return n * fact(n - 1)` is **not** a tail call: the multiplication happens after the call returns.
- `return fact_acc(n - 1, acc * n)` **is** a tail call.

You can often make a function tail-recursive by passing an **accumulator** that carries the partial result down:

```python
def fact_acc(n, acc=1):
    # Reject inputs outside the stated
    # domain.
    if type(n) is not int or n < 0:
        raise ValueError("nonnegative n")
    if n <= 1:
        return acc
    # Carry the product into the next call.
    return fact_acc(n - 1, acc * n)
```

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: passing on an enquiry
> At a help desk, one clerk takes your question, adds a note to your file and sends you to the next desk, then forgets about you: the next desk will give you the final answer. Another clerk sends you to the next desk but insists you come back so they can add a fee to whatever that desk tells you.
>
> **How it maps:** the first clerk is making a tail call: nothing is left to do after handing you on, so their desk (the frame) can be reused at once. The note in your file is the accumulator carrying the partial result forward. The second clerk is a non-tail call such as `n * fact(n - 1)`: their desk must stay occupied until the answer comes back.
>
> **Where it stops:** a clerk can always walk away. Whether a program actually frees the frame depends on the language implementation: Scheme guarantees it, C compilers may do it, and CPython never does.

Why care? Because a tail call needs nothing from the current frame afterwards, so a language can **reuse the frame** instead of pushing a new one. This is **tail-call optimisation (TCO)**, and it turns tail recursion into a loop with O(1) stack space. The Scheme programming language requires it by its standard; many functional language implementations rely on it; C compilers such as GCC and Clang often perform it at higher optimisation levels, but the C standard doesn't guarantee it.

### Python does not do TCO

CPython does not eliminate Python-level tail calls. `fact_acc(10000)` still raises `RecursionError` with the usual default allowance, accumulator or not.

Guido van Rossum explained the decision in 2009: eliminating frames would destroy useful **tracebacks**, and he considers recursion a less fundamental tool than iteration in Python. So in Python, rewriting as tail recursion does not by itself eliminate control-stack growth; its value is that it makes the next step, converting to a loop, mechanical.

## Key takeaways
- A tail call returns its result without pending work.
- An accumulator does not remove Python call frames; tail-call elimination is an implementation property.

## Further reading
- [Guido van Rossum: Tail Recursion Elimination](https://gvanrossum.github.io/neopythonic/tail-recursion-elimination.html)
- [Scheme standard](https://standards.scheme.org/r7rs-html5/index.html)

questions.prompt: Which of these `return` statements end in a **tail call** to `f`? Select all that apply.

options.text: `return f(n - 1, acc * n)`
options.explanation: Correct. The call's result is returned directly; nothing remains to do in the current frame.

options.text: `return 1 + f(n - 1)`
options.explanation: Not a tail call: after `f` returns, the frame must still add 1. The arithmetic around the call is pending work.

options.text: `return f(a) if a else f(b)`
options.explanation: Correct. Whichever branch is taken, the chosen call is the last action and its value is returned unchanged.

options.text: `return max(f(l), f(r))`
options.explanation: Not a tail call to `f`: both results must come back so `max` can compare them. Only the call to `max` is in tail position; the two calls to `f` are not.

options.text: `return n * f(n - 1)`
options.explanation: Not a tail call: the multiplication by n happens after the recursive call returns, so the frame must be kept.

questions.workedExample:
Ask one question of each call: *after it returns, is there anything left to do except return its value?*

| Statement | Work after call? | Tail? |
|---|---|---|
| `f(n-1, acc*n)` | none | yes |
| `1 + f(n-1)` | add 1 | no |
| `f(a) if a else f(b)` | none | yes |
| `max(f(l), f(r))` | compare | no |
| `n * f(n-1)` | multiply | no |

Note that `acc * n` is evaluated *before* the call, so it doesn't count as pending work.

options.text: It returns 5000! quickly, because the tail call reuses the frame
options.explanation: Scheme guarantees proper tail recursion, so control-stack growth is avoided; that does not by itself guarantee a particular execution speed. CPython has no such optimisation, so every call gets a new frame.

options.text: It raises RecursionError
options.explanation: Correct. CPython keeps one frame per call regardless of tail position, so 5000 nested calls exceed the default limit of 1000.

options.text: It raises OverflowError because 5000! is too big
options.explanation: Python integers are arbitrary precision; 5000! (over 16,000 digits) is computed fine by a loop. The problem is call depth, not integer size.

options.text: It works, because the recursion limit only counts non-tail calls
options.explanation: The limit counts all active Python frames. CPython doesn't distinguish tail calls from any other call.

questions.workedExample:
1. The function is genuinely tail-recursive: `acc * n` is computed before the call, and the call's result is returned unchanged.
2. But CPython does no tail-call optimisation (Guido van Rossum rejected it, chiefly to preserve full tracebacks).
3. So `fact(5000)` needs about 5000 frames, and the default `sys.getrecursionlimit()` is 1000 → `RecursionError`.
4. The accumulator form's real value in Python is that it converts mechanically into a loop:

```python
def fact(n):
    acc = 1
    while n > 1:
        # Both new values use the old
        # parameters.
        n, acc = n - 1, acc * n
    return acc
```

lessons.title: Turning recursion into iteration
lessons.summary: Self tail calls become parameter updates in a loop.
lessons.body:
## Converting recursion to iteration

### Tail recursion becomes a loop

A tail-recursive function maps directly onto a `while` loop: the parameters become variables, and the tail call becomes reassignment.

```python
def fact_iter(n):
    # Reject inputs outside the stated
    # domain.
    if type(n) is not int or n < 0:
        raise ValueError("nonnegative n")
    acc = 1
    while n > 1:     # not yet base case
        # Both new values use the old
        # parameters.
        n, acc = n - 1, acc * n
    return acc
```

### General recursion needs an explicit stack

When there are several recursive calls or work after the call, replace the call stack with your own list. This pre-order traversal avoids the interpreter recursion limit; its maximum usable input is still constrained by memory and execution time:

```python
def preorder(root):
    out, stack = [], [root]
    while stack:
        # Resume the most recently queued
        # subtree.
        node = stack.pop()
        # An empty subtree contributes no
        # nodes.
        if node is None:
            continue
        # Record the parent before its
        # children.
        out.append(node.val)
        # push right first so left
        # is popped (visited) first
        stack.append(node.right)
        stack.append(node.left)
    return out
```

A Python list stores pending work in dynamically allocated memory. General simulations can retain a resume point or a visited flag; specialised traversals sometimes need fewer entries. This routine also stores O(n) output. Here depth is the maximum nesting of pending work. The following table counts control-stack entries, assuming constant-sized entries; it excludes retained data and output.

| Approach | Stack space | Clarity |
|---|---|---|
| Plain recursion | O(depth), capped | High |
| Tail rec. + TCO | O(1) | High |
| Loop replacing self tail calls | O(1) | Medium |
| Explicit stack | O(depth), heap | Lower |

## Key takeaways
- Self tail calls become parameter updates in a loop.
- General recursion needs explicit pending work; push right before left to reproduce pre-order.

## Further reading
- [Recursive algorithms — Erickson](https://jeffe.cs.illinois.edu/teaching/algorithms/book/01-recursion.pdf)
- [Python recursion allowance](https://docs.python.org/3/library/sys.html)

questions.prompt: Your recursive DFS works in tests but crashes in production with `RecursionError` on a graph that is one long chain of 50,000 nodes. What is the most robust fix?

options.text: Call `sys.setrecursionlimit(100_000)` at start-up
options.explanation: This raises the Python-level allowance but is not a portable resource guarantee. Since CPython 3.11 most pure Python calls avoid C stack growth; C-involving call paths and memory limits still matter.

options.text: Rewrite the DFS with an explicit stack (a Python list) in a loop
options.explanation: Correct. The explicit work list avoids Python recursion depth. On a simple chain it needs very few pending entries; the visited set still grows with the graph. Available memory must be sufficient.

options.text: Rewrite it in tail-recursive form with an accumulator
options.explanation: CPython never eliminates tail calls, so a tail-recursive version uses exactly as many frames and fails the same way.

options.text: Add `@functools.lru_cache` to the DFS function
options.explanation: Caching avoids repeated work, but this crash is about depth, not repetition. The first call down the chain still nests 50,000 frames.

questions.workedExample:
1. Diagnose: the crash is caused by **recursion depth**. A 50,000-node chain makes the DFS nest 50,000 calls, far beyond the default limit of 1000.
2. Raising the limit changes one guard. It does not remove memory limits or C-stack risks on call paths that consume C stack; most pure Python calls since 3.11 avoid that growth.
3. Tail recursion doesn't help in CPython, which keeps every frame.
4. Replace the call stack with a list:

```python
stack, seen = [start], {start}
while stack:
    u = stack.pop()
    for v in graph[u]:
        if v not in seen:
            seen.add(v)
            stack.append(v)
```

For this mark-on-push graph traversal, pending entries and the visited set use O(V) additional storage. On general graphs its visitation tree need not equal recursive DFS; it solves the chain-depth problem here.

questions.prompt:
What does this print for the tree below?

```
      A

    B   C
   / \   \
  D   E   F
```

```python
out, stack = [], [root]
while stack:
    n = stack.pop()
    out.append(n.val)
    if n.right:
        # Right waits below the left
        # child.
        stack.append(n.right)
    if n.left:
        stack.append(n.left)
print("".join(out))
```

options.explanation: This is level order (BFS), which needs a queue. A stack processes the most recently pushed node first, so it goes deep before wide.

options.text: ACFBED
options.explanation: This would happen if left were pushed before right: right would be on top and visited first. The code pushes right first so that left is popped first.

options.text: ABDECF
options.explanation: Correct. Pushing right then left leaves the left child on top, so the loop visits node, left subtree, right subtree: pre-order.

Trace the stack (top on the right):

```

pop B  out=AB     push E, D  [C, E, D]
pop D  out=ABD               [C, E]
pop E  out=ABDE              [C]
pop C  out=ABDEC  push F     [F]
pop F  out=ABDECF            []
```

Pushing right before left is the standard trick that makes an explicit stack reproduce recursive pre-order exactly.

questions.prompt: Which statements about converting recursion to iteration are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: A tail-recursive function can be turned into a `while` loop by reassigning its parameters, with O(1) control-stack space (excluding retained argument data)
options.explanation: Correct. Nothing in the frame is needed after a tail call, so the call becomes 'update the variables and go round again'.

options.text: Any recursive function can be made iterative by managing an explicit stack of pending work
options.explanation: Correct. The call stack is just a stack; you can always simulate it, at worst by storing each frame's locals and a 'resume point'.

options.text: Converting to an explicit stack reduces the algorithm's space complexity
options.explanation: Usually false. You still store O(depth) entries; you've only moved them from the limited call stack to the heap.

options.text: In the lesson’s traversal, which pushes both children onto a LIFO stack, pushing right before left reproduces recursive pre-order
options.explanation: Correct. The stack is LIFO, so the child pushed last is visited first; pushing left last makes it come out first.

options.text: Iterative versions are always faster in CPython than recursive ones
options.explanation: Often somewhat faster because Python calls are expensive, but not 'always' and not asymptotically. The main reason to convert is the recursion limit.

questions.workedExample:
Go through each claim:

1. **Tail recursion → loop**: true. `f(n-1, acc*n)` becomes `n, acc = n-1, acc*n`.
2. **Explicit stack is universal**: true. This is a control-flow simulation; compilers can additionally optimise it; you can store `(node, state)` pairs to remember whether a frame has visited its left child yet.
3. **Space complexity drops**: false. Simulating every frame can retain linear space on a chain, but a specialised pre-order traversal can hold only constant pending work there. Converting does not universally improve the asymptotic bound.
4. **Push order**: true, because of LIFO.
5. **Always faster**: false as a universal claim. Relative timings depend on implementation and workload; conversion alone does not imply an asymptotic improvement.

lessons.title: Divide, conquer and combine
lessons.summary: Independent smaller pieces can be solved separately and combined.
lessons.body:
**Divide and conquer** is recursion with a plan. You divide the input into smaller subproblems, solve them recursively, and combine their answers. Balanced pieces often give efficient recurrences, but unequal splits also count as divide and conquer.

The payoff comes from the cutting. Halving an input of a million items takes only about 20 levels to reach size 1. So even if every level does work proportional to the whole input, the total is about 20 million basic steps, against about half a trillion comparisons for an algorithm that compares every item with every other item. These are scale estimates, not exact instruction counts or timings.

## The three steps

1. **Divide** the input into some number of smaller subproblems, each a fixed fraction of the original size.
2. **Conquer** each subproblem recursively (with a base case for tiny inputs).
3. **Combine** the sub-answers into the answer for the whole.

The cleanest examples have **independent** subproblems that can be solved separately. Repeated equivalent subproblems can waste work; caching them leads toward dynamic programming. Independence alone neither guarantees balanced splits nor eliminates all coordination costs in parallel implementations.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: counting votes in an election
> Each polling district counts its own ballots, the districts report to their region, and the regions report to a national total. Nobody needs to see another district's ballots to do their part.
>
> **How it maps:** splitting the country into districts is the divide step; each district's count is an independent subproblem; adding the reported totals is the combine step. Because districts don't overlap, no ballot is counted twice, which is what "independent subproblems" means.
>
> **Where it stops:** an election splits the country once into fixed districts. A divide-and-conquer algorithm keeps splitting the same way until pieces are tiny, and its combine step can be much more expensive than adding two numbers, as merging sorted lists or checking a boundary strip shows.

## Analysing it: recurrences

The cost of a divide-and-conquer algorithm is a **recurrence**: an equation that gives the running time on an input in terms of the running time on smaller inputs. Its shape is the relationship the rest of this module reasons about:

```formula essential
T(n) = aT(n / b) + f(n)
where
T(n): the running time on an input of size n, in basic steps
n: the input size (number of items, digits or points)
a: the number of subproblems each call creates; a fixed number of at least 1
b: the factor by which the input shrinks; each subproblem has size n / b; a fixed number greater than 1
T(n / b): the running time of one subproblem
f(n): the work one call does itself, outside its recursive calls: dividing the input and combining the answers
In words: one call costs the cost of its a smaller calls, plus the work it does itself to split and to combine.
```

Merge sort, for example, makes two half-size calls and does linear work to merge their answers.

Draw the recursion tree to see where the time goes. Going down one level multiplies the number of calls by a and divides each call's input size by b. Whether the total is dominated by the root, by the leaves or spread evenly depends on which of those two effects wins: how fast the number of calls grows compared with how fast the per-call work shrinks. The next unit turns that race into a rule.

## Key takeaways
- Independent smaller pieces can be solved separately and combined.
- Repeated equivalent subproblems call for caching rather than repeated plain recursion.

## Further reading
- [Recursive algorithms — Erickson](https://jeffe.cs.illinois.edu/teaching/algorithms/book/01-recursion.pdf)
- [Divide and conquer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divide-and-conquer_algorithm)

questions.prompt: Which of these problems are a good fit for plain divide and conquer (independent subproblems, no repeated work)? Select all that apply.

options.text: Finding the maximum element of an unsorted array by splitting it in half
options.explanation: Correct. The max of each half is independent of the other, and combining is one comparison. (It's O(n) for n elements, the same as a loop, but a natural fit for parallel execution.)

options.text: Counting inversions in an array during merge sort
options.explanation: Correct. Inversions within each half are counted recursively; cross inversions are counted during the merge. Classic O(n log n) divide and conquer, for n elements.

options.text: Computing the nth Fibonacci number as fib(n−1) + fib(n−2)
options.explanation: The two subproblems overlap heavily (fib(n−1) itself calls fib(n−2)), so naive recursion repeats work exponentially. That's dynamic programming territory.

options.text: Computing xⁿ by squaring x^(n/2)
options.explanation: Correct. One subproblem of half the size, constant-many arithmetic operations per combine: O(log n) operations for exponent n, with bit costs additional.

options.text: Finding the cheapest route through a grid with only right/down moves, using best costs of predecessor cells
options.explanation: The subproblems (best cost from each cell) are shared by many routes, so they overlap. That calls for DP, not divide and conquer.

questions.workedExample:
The test: *do the subproblems share sub-subproblems?*

- **Max of halves**: disjoint halves. ✓
- **Inversions**: disjoint halves plus a linear merge that counts cross pairs. ✓
- **Fibonacci**: fib(5) needs fib(4) and fib(3), and fib(4) needs fib(3) again. ✗ Overlapping.
- **Fast power**: a single subproblem; nothing to overlap. ✓
- **Grid paths**: the best cost from cell (i, j) is reused by every path through it. ✗ Overlapping.

Independent subproblems → divide and conquer. Overlapping subproblems → memoise or use DP.

lessons.title: Using the simplified master theorem
lessons.summary: Compare the exponent of local work with the critical leaf-growth exponent.
lessons.body:
The previous unit wrote a divide-and-conquer cost as the work of a smaller calls on inputs shrunk by a factor b, plus the work f(n) one call does itself. Here n is the input size. This unit compares those two effects to solve a restricted family of recurrences in one step.

Going down the recursion tree, two things happen at once:

- the **number of calls** multiplies by a at every level, so the bottom level ends up with a very large number of leaves;
- the **work per call** shrinks, because each input is b times smaller.

If the per-call work shrinks faster than the calls multiply, the root's own work dominates. If the calls multiply faster, the leaves dominate. If the two balance, every level costs about the same and you pay that once per level.

### The master theorem (simplified)

The **master theorem** settles that race for recurrences of this shape. It applies when a and b are fixed numbers, the base case costs a constant, and the work outside the recursion is a power of n. This simplified form ignores the rounding of subproblem sizes to whole numbers:

```formula essential
f(n) = Θ(n^d)
c = log_b(a)
T(n) = Θ(n^d)            if d > c
T(n) = Θ(n^d log(n))    if d = c
T(n) = Θ(n^c)            if d < c
where
T(n): the running time on an input of size n
n: the input size
f(n): the work one call does outside its recursive calls
d: the exponent of that work; a fixed number of at least 0 (d = 1 means linear work, d = 0 constant work)
n^d: n raised to the power d
a: the number of subproblems per call, at least 1
b: the factor by which each subproblem shrinks, greater than 1
c: the critical exponent: the number of leaves of the recursion tree grows like n^c
log_b(a): the logarithm of a to base b, the power you must raise b to in order to get a; for example log_2(4) = 2
log: logarithm; in Big-O and Big-Theta the base only changes a constant factor
Θ: Big-Theta, "grows at exactly this rate, up to constant factors"
In words: if the root's own work grows faster than the number of leaves, the root wins; if they match, every level costs the same and you pay that once per level, log n times; if the leaves grow faster, the leaves win.
```

| Case | Who dominates |
|---|---|
| combine exponent bigger | the root's combine |
| exponents equal | every level equally |
| leaf exponent bigger | the leaves |

You rarely need to compute anything beyond comparing two small numbers. The algorithms in the following units all fit this shape:

| Algorithm | Calls × size, local work | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Binary search | 1 × half, constant | logarithmic |
| Merge sort | 2 × half, linear | n log n |
| Closest pair | 2 × half, linear | n log n |
| Four-product multiply | 4 × half, linear | quadratic |
| Karatsuba | 3 × half, linear | n to the 1.585 |

Two patterns are worth remembering. Halving the input while keeping one call and constant work (binary search) is the equal case: constant work on each of about log n levels. Keeping linear work but adding more half-size calls pushes the recurrence into the leaves-dominate case, where the number of calls matters more than the combining.

More general recurrences (uneven splits, or local work growing linearly times a logarithm) need other tools, such as the full master theorem or the Akra–Bazzi method.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: who does most of the work in a company
> A director splits a job among a few managers and spends some time coordinating; each manager splits their part among their own team and coordinates that; and so on down to front-line staff who just do a small task each.
>
> **How it maps:** each person is a call, the number of direct reports is a, how much smaller each person's share is gives b, and coordination time is the local work f(n). If coordination at the top is heavy and shares shrink quickly, the director's level costs the most (root dominates). If the organisation spreads out so fast that front-line staff vastly outnumber everyone else, their combined effort dominates (leaves dominate). If each layer's total effort is the same, the cost is that amount times the number of layers.
>
> **Where it stops:** real organisations are irregular. The theorem only applies when every call has exactly the same branching factor, the same shrink factor and local work that is a power of the input size.

## Key takeaways
- Compare the exponent of local work with the critical leaf-growth exponent.
- The simplified theorem assumes fixed branching and shrink factors and power-shaped local work.

## Further reading
- [Recursive cost analysis — Erickson](https://jeffe.cs.illinois.edu/teaching/algorithms/book/01-recursion.pdf)
- [Master theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master_theorem_(analysis_of_algorithms))

questions.prompt:
Using the simplified master theorem, what is the tight bound for this recurrence? (This is splitting each number in half and doing all four products, before Karatsuba's trick.)

```formula
T(n) = 4T(n / 2) + Θ(n)
T(1) = Θ(1)
where
T(n): the cost of multiplying two n-digit numbers
n: the number of digits
Θ(n): linear work, for the additions and shifts
Θ(1): constant work, for one-digit numbers
Θ: Big-Theta, exactly this growth rate up to constant factors
In words: each call makes four half-size calls and does linear work of its own.
```

options.text: Linear times a logarithm
options.explanation: That's the case where the number of subproblems equals the shrink factor (like merge sort: 2 halves of size n/2, n being the input size). Here there are 4 subproblems of size n/2, so the leaves multiply much faster than the work per level shrinks.

options.text: Quadratic
options.explanation: Correct. Four half-size calls have a critical exponent of two, greater than the linear combine exponent of one, so the leaves dominate with quadratic cost.

options.text: The three-product Karatsuba growth rate
options.explanation: Karatsuba has three half-size calls, whose critical exponent is about 1.585. Four calls instead give a critical exponent of two.

options.text: Linear
options.explanation: The combine step is linear, but the fourfold branching at each level produces quadratic total leaf work.

questions.workedExample:
Here n is the number of digits.

1. Read off the shape: four calls, each on half the digits, with linear local work, so the local-work exponent is 1.
2. Critical exponent: how many times must you double to get 4? Twice, so the leaves grow like n squared and the critical exponent is 2.
3. Compare: 2 is bigger than 1, so this is the **leaves dominate** case, and the cost is **quadratic**, no better than schoolbook multiplication.

Recursion-tree view: each level has four times as many calls, each on half as many digits, so each level does about twice the work of the level above. The bottom level, with about n² one-digit products, dominates the total.

Karatsuba's three half-size products change the critical exponent to about 1.585, which is why removing one product beats any constant-factor saving: it changes the growth rate.

lessons.title: Binary search and one shrinking subproblem
lessons.summary: Use the master theorem to count midpoint probes when only one half survives.
lessons.body:
Here n is the number of sorted items. The previous unit compared local work with leaf growth; binary search is its equal-exponent case with just one surviving half at each step.

### Binary search

Compare the target with the middle element and discard the half that can't contain it. That leaves **one** subproblem of half the size, and each call does only a constant amount of work: one probe and comparison.

In master-theorem terms there is a single call (so the number of calls never grows) and constant local work, which is the "every level equal" case. Constant work on each of about log₂ n levels gives a **logarithmic** running time.

What that means in practice:

- A billion sorted items need at most **30** midpoint probes: each probe halves the remaining range, and 2 to the power 30 is just over a billion.
- **Doubling** the data adds just **one** more probe: the first comparison cuts the doubled range back to the old size.
- Ten halvings shrink the range about a thousandfold, so every factor of a thousand in data costs about ten more probes.

```formula reference
p_max = floor(log_2(n)) + 1
where
p_max: the maximum number of midpoint probes ordinary binary search makes on a non-empty sorted range
n: the number of items in the range
floor: round down to the nearest whole number
log_2: the base-two logarithm: the number of times you can halve a number before reaching 1
In words: the worst case is one probe per halving, plus the final probe on a single remaining item; a billion items need at most thirty.
```

A three-way comparator can classify a probe in one comparison; separate equality and ordering tests may perform more.

Binary search is the degenerate case where "combine" is free and one half is thrown away entirely. Some people call this *decrease and conquer*.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: finding a name in a printed phone book
> You open the book near the middle, see whether the name you want comes before or after that page, and ignore the other half of the book. Then you repeat with the half you kept.
>
> **How it maps:** opening a page is a midpoint probe; alphabetical order is the sorted-input requirement that makes discarding half safe; each look roughly halves what is left, so even a huge book needs only a couple of dozen looks.
>
> **Where it stops:** people jump closer to the right letter (for "W" they open near the back), which is closer to interpolation search. Binary search always probes the exact middle, and it only works when the data really is sorted by the same key you compare.

## Key takeaways
- A midpoint comparison discards one half and leaves no costly combination.
- Count midpoint probes separately from language-level equality and ordering tests.

## Further reading
- [Recursive cost analysis — Erickson](https://jeffe.cs.illinois.edu/teaching/algorithms/book/01-recursion.pdf)

questions.prompt: Binary search on a sorted array of one billion elements needs at most about 30 midpoint probes, counting one three-way comparison per probe. The array grows to **two billion** elements. Roughly how many probes does the worst case need now?

options.text: About 60
options.explanation: Doubling the probe count would be right for linear search, whose work grows in step with the data. Binary search's work grows with the number of halvings, which rises by only one.

options.text: About 45
options.explanation: There is no square-root or partial scaling here. Each probe halves the range, so a doubled range needs exactly one extra halving.

options.text: About 31
options.explanation: Correct. The first probe cuts two billion candidates to one billion, and from there the search behaves exactly as before: one extra probe.

options.text: About 30, because the logarithm hardly changes
options.explanation: Close in spirit, but the change is not zero. A doubled range always needs one more halving to get back to the old size.

questions.workedExample:
1. Binary search keeps one half-size subproblem and does constant work per probe, so its probe count follows the number of halvings needed to shrink the range to one item.
2. For two billion items, the first probe discards one billion of them. What remains is a one-billion-item search, which needs at most about 30 probes.
3. So the worst case is about **31** probes.

The general pattern: each doubling of the data adds one probe, and each thousandfold increase adds about ten (2 to the power 10 is 1024). That is what logarithmic growth feels like in practice.

lessons.title: Merge sort as divide and conquer
lessons.summary: Two sorted halves can be merged in linear work per level.
lessons.body:
For this unit n is the number of items being sorted. Merge sort is a concrete example of two independent half-size problems followed by linear combination.

### Merge sort

Split the list in half, sort each half, and merge the two sorted halves in linear time.

```python
def merge_sort(xs):
    if len(xs) <= 1:
        return xs
    mid = len(xs) // 2
    # Each copied half is sorted
    # independently.
    left = merge_sort(xs[:mid])
    right = merge_sort(xs[mid:])
    out, i, j = [], 0, 0
    while i < len(left) and j < len(right):
        # Use the left equal key to retain
        # stability.
        if left[i] <= right[j]:
            out.append(left[i]); i += 1
        else:
            out.append(right[j]); j += 1
    # Only one sorted remainder can be non-
    # empty.
    return out + left[i:] + right[j:]
```

```
level 0:  [ 8 3 5 1 ]          n work
level 1:  [ 8 3 ]  [ 5 1 ]     n work
level 2:  [8] [3]  [5] [1]     n work
          3 levels, all 4 items each
```

Each level does linear work in total (every item is merged once per level), and there are about log₂n + 1 levels. In master-theorem terms, two half-size calls balance a linear merge exactly: the "every level equal" case.

```formula reference
T(n) = 2T(n / 2) + Θ(n)
T(n) = Θ(n log(n))
where
T(n): the running time of merge sort on n items
n: the number of items to sort
Θ(n): work proportional to n, here the merge, which touches every item once
log: logarithm (the base only changes a constant)
Θ: Big-Theta, grows at exactly this rate up to constant factors
In words: two half-size sorts plus a linear merge cost the same on every level, and there are about log n levels, so the total grows like n log n.
```

For a million items, the linear-times-logarithm scale is roughly twenty million. This is neither an exact element-move count nor a timing; copied slices and concatenations also contribute work. The `<=` ensures a **stable sort** (equal keys stay in their original order). The price is O(n) extra memory for merging.

## Key takeaways
- Two sorted halves can be merged in linear work per level.
- Stable merging uses the left element on equal keys, and ordinary merging needs linear extra storage.

## Further reading
- [Recursive sorting — Erickson](https://jeffe.cs.illinois.edu/teaching/algorithms/book/01-recursion.pdf)

For a million items that is about 20 levels of a million steps each: a scale estimate, not an exact comparison count.

lessons.title: Fast and modular exponentiation
lessons.summary: Compute the half-power once, then square it.
lessons.body:
## Fast exponentiation

To raise a number x to a non-negative whole-number power n, straightforward powering multiplies by x one time after another, which is O(n) multiplications. The bounds here count arithmetic operations; large-integer bit costs are additional. Divide and conquer notices that a power splits into two equal halves:

```formula essential
x^n = (x^{n/2})^2        if n mod 2 = 0
x^n = (x^{⌊n/2⌋})^2 x  if n mod 2 = 1
where
x: the base, the number being raised to a power
n: the exponent, a whole number of at least 0
x^n: n copies of x multiplied together (x^0 = 1)
mod: the remainder after division (Python's %); n mod 2 is 0 when n is even and 1 when n is odd
(…)^2: squaring: the bracketed value multiplied by itself
⌊n/2⌋: the floor of n / 2: halve n and round down to a whole number (Python's n // 2); ⌊7/2⌋ = 3
In words: to get x to the n, compute x to half of n once and square it; if n is odd, the rounding down lost one factor of x, so multiply it back in.
```

For example, x to the 7 is x cubed squared, times one more x; and x cubed is x squared times x. Each step halves the exponent.

```python
def power(x, n):
    # Reject inputs outside the stated
    # domain.
    if type(n) is not int or n < 0:
        raise ValueError("nonnegative n")
    if n == 0:
        return 1
    # Reuse this result instead of calling
    # twice.
    half = power(x, n // 2)   # once!
    if n % 2 == 0:
        return half * half
    return half * half * x
```

Each call halves n, so there are about log₂n calls, each doing at most two multiplications: one half-size call with constant work, the logarithmic case of the master theorem. Raising x to the millionth power takes 20 squarings plus a few extra multiplications for odd steps, instead of 999,999 multiplications.

> [!warning] Compute the half once
> Writing `return power(x, n // 2) * power(x, n // 2)` makes two recursive calls instead of one. You've rebuilt the slow algorithm with extra overhead.

The recurrence shows why: two calls on half the exponent, with constant work each, is the "leaves dominate" case. The call tree doubles at every level for about log₂n levels, so it ends with about n leaves, and the total is linear in n: no better than multiplying n times.

The iterative version reads the bits of n from least significant upwards: square x at every step and multiply it into the result when the bit is 1.

```python
def power_iter(x, n):
    # Reject inputs outside the stated
    # domain.
    if type(n) is not int or n < 0:
        raise ValueError("nonnegative n")
    result = 1
    while n > 0:
        # A set exponent bit contributes
        # this power.
        if n & 1:
            result *= x
        # Advance to the next squared power.
        x *= x
        # Discard the exponent bit just
        # consumed.
        n >>= 1
    return result
```

With a modulus applied after every multiplication, this is **modular exponentiation**, the workhorse of RSA and Diffie–Hellman. Taking the remainder after each step keeps the numbers small, and it gives the same final remainder as computing the huge power first. For example, three to the 13th is 1,594,323, which leaves remainder 3 when divided by 7; the loop reaches the same 3 without ever holding a number bigger than 36.

```formula reference
(ab) mod m
  = ((a mod m) × (b mod m)) mod m
where
a: one number being multiplied
b: the other number being multiplied
m: the modulus, a positive whole number
mod: the remainder after dividing by m (Python's %); 17 mod 7 = 3
In words: you can reduce each factor to its remainder before multiplying and still get the right remainder at the end. So every intermediate product stays below the square of the modulus, once the starting base has been reduced too.
```

Python’s built-in `pow(base, exp, mod)` performs efficient modular powering; CPython 3.14 uses binary powering and a sliding-window method depending on exponent size. It is not literally this loop. Fixed-size matrix powering can compute the nth Fibonacci number using O(log n) matrix multiplications, with growing integer bit costs.

## Key takeaways
- Compute the half-power once, then square it.
- Reducing products modulo a positive modulus preserves the final remainder.

## Further reading
- [Python pow](https://docs.python.org/3/library/functions.html#pow)
- [Pinned CPython 3.14 integer implementation](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/python/cpython/v3.14.0/Objects/longobject.c)

options.explanation: There's no linear work per level here, only a constant number of multiplications per call.

options.explanation: Correct. For an exponent n, the duplicate half-power calls create linearly many calls in the unit-cost model. Odd arguments take an extra decrement step; when n is a power of two every call below the top is even, so the two-half-calls pattern applies all the way down.

options.text: Quadratic
options.explanation: Quadratic cost would need about n calls each doing linear work, or about n² calls. Here every call does a constant number of multiplications and the call tree has only about n leaves, so the total is linear.

For integer arguments, trace the iterative fast power with a positive modulus. What does it return?

```python
def powmod(x, n, m):
    if n < 0 or m <= 0:
        raise ValueError("domain")
    result = 1 % m
    while n > 0:
        # A set exponent bit contributes
        # this power.
        if n & 1:
            # Include this set exponent
            # bit.
            result = result * x % m
        # Square the base for the next
        # bit.
        x = x * x % m
        # Discard the exponent bit just
        # consumed.
        n >>= 1

powmod(3, 13, 7)
```

options.explanation: Correct. The set exponent bits select the eighth, fourth and first powers of three. The remainders after dividing by 7 are 2, 4 and 3, and 2 × 4 × 3 = 24, which leaves remainder 3.
One is the remainder of the sixth and twelfth powers of three after division by seven. This misses the final multiply for the lowest bit set in 13 = 1101₂.
5 is the value of `result` part-way through (after the 3⁴ step). The loop still has one more set bit to process.

6 is what you get if the base is never squared: each set bit then multiplies by plain 3, so 3 × 3 × 3 = 27, which leaves remainder 6. Squaring x every iteration is what makes the three set bits of 13 select the first, fourth and eighth powers.

```
13   1    1*3=3        3*3=9%7=2
6    0    3            2*2=4
3    1    3*4=12%7=5   4*4=16%7=2

```

Result **3**. A cross-check without the loop: three to the sixth is 729, which leaves remainder 1 when divided by 7 (Fermat's little theorem). Thirteen is two sixes plus one, so three to the 13th leaves the same remainder as plain 3.

Python’s `pow(3, 13, 7)` agrees. The displayed loop uses four squarings and three result multiplications in four iterations; the built-in need not use the same loop.

lessons.title: Karatsuba and fewer products
lessons.summary: Three recursive half-products replace the four products of schoolbook splitting.
lessons.body:
## Karatsuba multiplication

Schoolbook multiplication of two n-digit numbers multiplies every digit of one by every digit of the other: O(n²) digit products. In 1960 Anatoly Karatsuba found a faster way, published with Ofman in 1962.

Split each number into a high half and a low half around a power of ten. Their product then has three parts: the two high halves multiplied together, the two low halves multiplied together, and a middle part made of the two cross products. The trick is that the middle part can be had with **one** extra multiplication instead of two:

```formula essential
x = a 10^m + b
y = c 10^m + d
xy = ac × 10^{2m} + (ad + bc) × 10^m + bd
ad + bc = (a + b)(c + d) − ac − bd
where
x: the first number to multiply, with n digits
y: the second number to multiply, with n digits
n: the number of digits in each number
m: the split point, about half the number of digits (n / 2)
10^m: 10 raised to the power m, a 1 followed by m zeros
10^{2m}: 10 raised to the power 2m
a: the high half of x (its leading digits)
b: the low half of x (its last m digits)
c: the high half of y
d: the low half of y
In words: the product is "high × high" shifted left by 2m digits, plus the cross terms shifted by m digits, plus "low × low". Multiply the two half-sums once and subtract the high and low products you already have: what remains is exactly the sum of the cross terms.
```

So Karatsuba computes only three half-size products: ac, bd and the product of the half-sums. Additions, subtractions and shifts are cheap, linear-time operations.

### Why one product matters

- **Four half-size products** (ac, ad, bc and bd separately) with linear extra work is the master theorem's "leaves dominate" case with a critical exponent of 2: quadratic, no better than schoolbook.
- **Three half-size products** lower the critical exponent to log₂3, about 1.585. The cost grows like n to that power.

Dropping one product is not a constant-factor saving: it changes the growth rate. Each time the digit count doubles, Karatsuba's work roughly triples while schoolbook's quadruples. For 1000-digit numbers the scale expressions are about 57,000 against a million. Those are growth-model figures, not exact digit-product counts: rounding, base cases and carries in the half-sums all matter.

```formula reference
T(n) = 3T(n / 2) + O(n)
T(n) = Θ(n^{log_2(3)})
where
T(n): the number of digit operations to multiply two n-digit numbers
n: the number of digits in each number
O(n): linear work for the additions, subtractions and shifts
log_2(3): the base-2 logarithm of 3, about 1.585
Θ: Big-Theta, grows at exactly this rate up to constant factors
In words: three half-size products plus linear work put the algorithm in the "leaves dominate" case, with about n^1.585 work instead of n^2.
```

A worked example on 1234 × 5678, splitting after two digits: the high halves are 12 and 56, the low halves 34 and 78. Three two-digit products are needed: 12 × 56 = 672, 34 × 78 = 2652, and the half-sums 46 × 134 = 6164. The middle part is 6164 − 672 − 2652 = 2840. Shifting and adding gives 6,720,000 + 284,000 + 2,652 = 7,006,652, the correct product.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: measuring a room by subtraction
> A rectangular room is divided by one line across and one line down into four rectangular zones. A carpet fitter already knows the areas of two diagonally opposite zones and needs the combined area of the other two. Instead of measuring each of those, they measure the whole room once and subtract the two areas they already have.
>
> **How it maps:** the room's sides are the half-sums (a + b) and (c + d), so its area is their product, which contains all four zones ac, ad, bc and bd. The two known zones are ac and bd. Subtracting them leaves the other two together, ad + bc, at the cost of one measurement instead of two.
>
> **Where it stops:** for a carpet fitter, one saved measurement is a small convenience. In Karatsuba the saving repeats at every level of the recursion, which is what changes the growth rate; and the subtraction only gives the two zones' total, never each one separately, which is all the product needs.

## Key takeaways
- Three recursive half-products replace the four products of schoolbook splitting.
- Arithmetic-operation counts, bit costs and real implementation cutoffs are different claims.

## Further reading
- [Karatsuba algorithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karatsuba_algorithm)
- [GMP multiplication algorithms](https://gmplib.org/manual/Multiplication-Algorithms)

Karatsuba splits x into high and low halves a and b, and y into c and d. For the middle coefficient, the sum of the two cross products a × d and b × c, it computes one product of half-sums and subtracts:

```formula
p_mid = (a + b)(c + d) − ac − bd
where
p_mid: the middle coefficient, a × d + b × c
a: the high half of x
b: the low half of x
c: the high half of y
d: the low half of y
In words: one product of the half-sums, minus the high and low products, gives the middle coefficient.
```

Why does it subtract ac and bd, and what does that buy?

options.text: To correct carries between the digit blocks, so the halves can be added without overflow
options.explanation: Carries are handled by the final shifted additions, not by this subtraction. The subtraction removes whole products, not carry digits.

options.text: To avoid ever multiplying numbers longer than half the original
options.explanation: The half-sums can be one digit longer than a half, so this product can be slightly bigger. Avoiding that is not the purpose; saving a multiplication is.

options.text: Because the cross products are negative and must be subtracted
options.explanation: For non-negative inputs every product here is non-negative. Nothing is subtracted because of its sign.

options.text: The half-sum product contains ac and bd as well as the cross terms; both are already needed, so subtracting them leaves the cross terms with three products instead of four
options.explanation: Correct. Expanding (a + b)(c + d) gives ac + ad + bc + bd. Since ac and bd are computed anyway, one extra product yields ad + bc, and three half-size products change the growth rate from quadratic to about n to the power 1.585 for n digits.

questions.workedExample:
1. The full product needs three pieces: ac (shifted furthest left), the cross terms ad + bc (shifted by half the digits), and bd.
2. Computing ad and bc separately would take four half-size multiplications in total, which is the quadratic "leaves dominate" case.
3. Multiplying the half-sums gives ac + ad + bc + bd in one multiplication.
4. ac and bd are needed for the final answer anyway, so subtracting them costs only additions and subtractions and leaves exactly ad + bc.

Small check with 21 × 43: the half-sum product is 3 × 7 = 21, the high and low products are 8 and 3, and 21 − 8 − 3 = 10, which equals 2 × 3 + 1 × 4. The pieces 800 + 100 + 3 give 903, the correct product.

lessons.title: Implementing Karatsuba and matrix splitting
lessons.summary: Binary splits implement the same three-product algebra.
lessons.body:
The previous unit derived Karatsuba: combine the high-half product, low-half product and one product of half-sums. Here we implement that algebra with binary splits, then see the same "fewer multiplications" idea in square matrix multiplication.

The preceding algebra unit uses decimal blocks for readability. This implementation splits at powers of two, avoiding decimal string conversion and its input-size limit. Its recurrence counts bit operations on linearly sized additions/splits.

```python
def karatsuba(x, y):
    if (type(x) is not int
            or type(y) is not int):
        raise TypeError("integer operands")
    sign = -1 if (x < 0) != (y < 0) else 1
    def mul(x, y):
        if x < 16 or y < 16:
            return x * y
        m = max(x.bit_length(),
                y.bit_length()) // 2
        # Split at a binary block boundary.
        base = 1 << m
        a, b = divmod(x, base)
        c, d = divmod(y, base)
        # Keep both products for
        # reconstruction.
        ac, bd = mul(a, c), mul(b, d)
        # Subtract known products from the
        # half-sums.
        mid = mul(a + b, c + d) - ac - bd
        return ((ac << (2*m))
                + (mid << m) + bd)
    return sign * mul(abs(x), abs(y))
```

In practice the additions and subtractions make Karatsuba slower than schoolbook for small numbers. In CPython 3.14, ordinary multiplication uses Karatsuba only when both operands exceed 70 internal digits; the squaring cutoff is 140. Internal digits have 15 or 30 bits depending on the build (`sys.int_info.bits_per_digit`). Libraries such as GMP go further with Toom–Cook and FFT-based methods for very large numbers. The same "fewer multiplications" idea gives **Strassen's** matrix multiplication. Splitting two square matrices into quarter blocks naively needs 8 half-size block products; Strassen (1969) needs only 7, at the price of 18 block additions and subtractions. The additions cost work proportional to the number of entries, which is quadratic in the matrix side n, while the seven recursive products put the recurrence in the "leaves dominate" case. The result grows like n to the power log₂7, about n to the power 2.807, instead of the n³ of the schoolbook method. As with Karatsuba, practical libraries switch to it only above a size cutoff, if at all.

## Key takeaways
- Binary splits implement the same three-product algebra.
- Practical multiplication selects algorithms by operand size; matrix splitting has its own arithmetic model.

## Further reading
- [Pinned CPython 3.14 integer implementation](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/python/cpython/v3.14.0/Objects/longobject.c)
- [GMP multiplication algorithms](https://gmplib.org/manual/Multiplication-Algorithms)

Here n is the number of digits, and the model was calibrated to 1 ms for both methods at 1000 digits.

1. Going from 1000 to 4000 digits is two doublings (1000 → 2000 → 4000).
2. **Karatsuba**: doubling n multiplies the time by 2 to the power log₂(3), which is exactly 3. Two doublings give 3 × 3 = 9, so about **9 ms**.
3. **Schoolbook**: doubling n multiplies a quadratic time by 4. Two doublings give 16, so about **16 ms**.

The gap widens with size: at 64,000 digits (six doublings) the same model predicts 729 ms against 4,096 ms. These are model predictions, not measurements. Actual crossovers depend on implementation and hardware; CPython has explicit size cutoffs.

lessons.title: Why closest-pair checks seven neighbours
lessons.summary: Cross-half improvements must lie in a narrow strip.
lessons.body:
## Closest pair of points

Given n points in the plane, find the two closest. Brute force checks every pair: for a thousand points that is 499,500 pairs, and the number of pairs grows like n², so brute force is O(n²).

Divide and conquer does it in O(n log n) time, where n is still the number of points.

1. Sort the points by x once. Split them with a vertical line at the median x.
2. Recursively find the closest distance on each side. Call the smaller of the two answers δ (delta): the best distance found so far.
3. The only pairs left to check are those that **straddle** the line. A straddling pair closer than δ must have both points within δ of the line, in a strip of width 2δ (δ on each side).

```
         |<- δ ->|<- δ ->|
   .     |   .   |       |    .
     .   |       |  .    |
  .      |  .    |   .   |  .
         |     strip     |
           mid line
```

4. Maintain y order through the recursion; extract the strip in that order. Compare each point with the next **7** points.

## Why only 7 neighbours?

Fix a point p in the strip. Any partner closer than δ that comes after p in y order lies in a rectangle δ tall and 2δ wide just above p, straddling the line.

Split that rectangle into eight small squares, each δ/2 on a side: four on the left of the line and four on the right. Assign a point that sits exactly on the line to the half it came from, and look at each half's four squares separately.

The key fact is that **two points from the same half can't share a small square**. The furthest apart two points in a square can be is its diagonal, about 0.71δ, which is less than δ. But every pair within one half is at least δ apart, because δ is no bigger than that half's closest distance. So each small square holds at most one point of its half.

```formula reference
g = √(s^2 + s^2) = δ / √(2) ≈ 0.707δ
where
g: the length of a small square's diagonal, the furthest apart two points inside it can be
s: the side length of each small square, δ / 2
δ: delta, the smallest distance found within either half
√: the square root
≈: approximately equal to
In words: two points in the same small square are at most about 0.71 δ apart, which is closer than δ.
```

That allows at most eight points in the rectangle, one of which is p itself, leaving at most **7** others. Any point further along in y order is too far above p to beat δ. The bound is a proof for every input of distinct points, not a heuristic, and it keeps the combine step linear.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: socially distanced guests on square tiles
> At a reception where every guest must stand at least two metres from every other, a square tile whose diagonal is shorter than two metres can never hold two guests at once.
>
> **How it maps:** the guests are points from one half, the two-metre rule is "same-half points are at least δ apart", and the tiles are the δ/2 squares. Counting tiles near a guest bounds how many other guests can be close by, which is the "at most 7" bound.
>
> **Where it stops:** the distancing rule only applies within one half of the room, which is why each side's tiles are counted separately; a guest from the other side may stand closer than δ, and finding such a pair is exactly what the strip check is for.

## Key takeaways
- Cross-half improvements must lie in a narrow strip.
- Within each recursive half, small-square packing bounds the relevant neighbours.

## Further reading
- [Closest pair — Dartmouth notes](https://cs.dartmouth.edu/~deepc/LecNotes/cs31/lec7.pdf)

1. Any pair closer than δ that straddles the line must have both points within δ of the line.
2. Fix a point p in the strip. A closer partner q above p has a y-coordinate between p's y and that plus δ, and an x-coordinate within δ of the line: a rectangle δ tall and 2δ wide.

5. That's at most 8 points in the rectangle including p, so at most 7 others to check.

lessons.title: Keeping closest-pair combination linear
lessons.summary: Preserve y order throughout recursion rather than sorting every strip.
lessons.body:
The previous unit proved that the strip needs at most seven later neighbours per point. Here n is the number of points; px and py hold the same distinct points sorted by x and y. The implementation maintains that ordering so every combine stays linear.

The combine step is O(n), provided you keep a y-sorted list rather than re-sorting the strip at every level. Re-sorting costs O(n log n) per level, which would give O(n log² n) in total, where log is any fixed-base logarithm; the squared logarithm multiplies that logarithm by itself.

The implementation returns the minimum distance (infinity for fewer than two points). Coordinates must be finite real numbers with meaningful subtraction; `hypot` uses floating-point arithmetic, so exact geometric predicates would need a different numeric representation. Hash-based partitioning assumes expected constant-time tuple lookup.

```python
from math import hypot

def dist(p, q):
    return hypot(p[0] - q[0], p[1] - q[1])

def brute_force(points):
    return min((dist(p, q)
                for i, p
                in enumerate(points)
                for q in points[i+1:]),
               default=float("inf"))

def closest(points):
    points = [tuple(p) for p in points]
    # Coincident points make the distance
    # zero.
    if len(set(points)) != len(points):
        return 0.0
    py = sorted(points, key=lambda p: p[1])
    return _closest(sorted(points), py)

def _closest(px, py):    # distinct points
    n = len(px)
    if n <= 3:
        return brute_force(px)
    mid = n // 2
    mx = px[mid][0]
    lx, rx = px[:mid], px[mid:]
    lset = set(lx)
    # Partition while preserving y order.
    ly = [p for p in py if p in lset]
    ry = [p for p in py if p not in lset]
    d = min(_closest(lx, ly),
            _closest(rx, ry))
    strip = [p for p in py
             if abs(p[0] - mx) < d]
    for i, p in enumerate(strip):
        # The packing proof permits seven
        # neighbours.
        for q in strip[i+1:i+8]:
            d = min(d, dist(p, q))
    return d
```

## Key takeaways
- Preserve y order throughout recursion rather than sorting every strip.
- Finite distinct coordinates, floating-point distance and expected hash lookup are explicit implementation assumptions.

## Further reading
- [Closest pair — Dartmouth notes](https://cs.dartmouth.edu/~deepc/LecNotes/cs31/lec7.pdf)
- [Python hypot](https://docs.python.org/3/library/math.html#math.hypot)

options.explanation: The textbook O(n log n) relies on an O(n) combine step. Sorting the strip costs O(n log n) per level, which changes the recurrence.

options.text: O(n²)
options.explanation: Sorting is O(n log n), not O(n²), so each level costs O(n log n) at most. The linear-times-log-squared upper bound grows more slowly than a quadratic bound.

options.text: O(n log n · 7)
options.explanation: The 7-neighbour scan is linear; it's the per-level sort that adds the extra log factor, not the scan.

questions.workedExample:
Here n is the number of points in a call.

1. Combine cost per call: build the strip (linear), sort it (O(n log n) comparisons when the strip is linear in size), scan 7 neighbours per point (linear). The sort dominates.
2. The recursion still has about log n levels, and on each level the calls together hold n points.
3. Sorting the strips on one level therefore costs at most about n log n in total, and adding that over about log n levels gives at most n times log n squared: **O(n log² n)**, one log factor worse than the textbook version.

If every strip really is linear in its subproblem size and the sorting cost is tight, that upper bound is also attained; merely knowing an upper bound on each strip sort establishes the stated worst-case upper bound, without claiming that every input reaches it.

The fix is to sort by y **once** at the start and split the y-sorted list into left and right in linear time per call. Then the combine is O(n) and the total is O(n log n).
