lessons.title: Divide-and-conquer engineering tradeoffs
lessons.summary: Hybrid cutoffs and independent tasks can help in practice, with overhead still counted.
lessons.body:
The previous units analysed divide-and-conquer under explicit cost models. Here n denotes input size. Engineering decisions affect constants, memory and even the recurrence: changing a split or a combine can change the whole bound.

## In the real world

- **Hybrid cut-offs.** Recursion has overhead, so practical implementations switch to a simple algorithm below a threshold. Timsort (Python's `sorted`) uses insertion sort on short runs; CPython multiplies small integers the schoolbook way.
- **Parallelism.** Independent subproblems can run on different cores. Java’s fork/join framework can execute recursive divide-and-conquer tasks. MapReduce also separates local processing and aggregation, but a MapReduce job need not be a recursive divide-and-conquer algorithm.
- **External sorting.** Databases sort data bigger than RAM by sorting chunks that fit in memory and merging them: merge sort's structure.
- **Memory.** Merge sort needs O(n) extra space; quicksort is divide and conquer with all the work in the *divide* step (partitioning) and a trivial combine, using in-place partitioning; recursive stack space is additional.

## Pitfalls

- **Overlapping subproblems.** If the pieces share sub-pieces (naive Fibonacci), divide and conquer repeats work exponentially. That's a job for DP.
- **Unbalanced splits.** Quicksort with a bad pivot leaves one non-empty subproblem with only one item removed. For n original items, recursion can then have linear depth instead of logarithmic depth, and the partitioning work adds up to n, then n − 1, and so on: about n²/2 steps, so **Θ(n²)** instead of Θ(n log n).

- **An expensive combine.** The combine step decides the complexity. Re-sorting inside the recursion, or copying large slices, can quietly add a log factor or worse.

## Key takeaways
- Hybrid cutoffs and independent tasks can help in practice, with overhead still counted.
- Unbalanced splits and expensive combination can destroy the intended growth bound.

## Further reading
- [Java ForkJoinPool](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/util/concurrent/ForkJoinPool.html)
- [GMP multiplication algorithms](https://gmplib.org/manual/Multiplication-Algorithms)

questions.prompt: Which statements about divide and conquer in practice are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: Some production sort and multiplication routines switch to a simpler method for small inputs
options.explanation: Correct. Recursion and bookkeeping overhead dominate on tiny inputs. Timsort uses insertion sort on short runs; CPython uses schoolbook multiplication below its Karatsuba cutoff.

options.text: Strassen's algorithm multiplies matrices with 7 half-size products instead of 8, giving O(n^(log₂7))
options.explanation: Correct. For square matrices with n rows and n columns, seven half-size products plus quadratic block additions yield the exact critical exponent log₂(7), about 2.807.

options.text: Quicksort does its main work in the combine step
options.explanation: The reverse. Quicksort's work is in the divide step (partitioning around a pivot); its combine is trivial. Merge sort is the one with a trivial divide and a linear combine.

options.text: Independent subproblems make divide and conquer easy to parallelise
options.explanation: Correct. Independent subproblems can run concurrently, as in fork/join parallel merge sort. Task scheduling, shared resources and combining still impose costs.

options.text: Merge sort sorts in place with O(1) extra memory
options.explanation: Standard merge sort needs O(n) extra space for merging. In-place merging variants exist with different complexity and implementation tradeoffs; quicksort and heapsort are the usual in-place choices.

questions.workedExample:
Check each claim:

1. **Cut-offs**: true. Asymptotically faster isn't faster for small inputs; hybrids win.
2. **Strassen**: true. Seven half-size block products with quadratic block additions put the recurrence in the "leaves dominate" case, so the cost grows like n to the power log₂7, about n to the power 2.807, for n × n matrices.
3. **Quicksort's work**: false. In-place partition = divide; the two sorted ranges already occupy their final positions, so no concatenation is needed. Allocating concatenation would not be free.
4. **Parallelism**: true. Independent subproblems permit concurrent work, but scheduling and shared-resource coordination may still be needed.
5. **Merge sort in place**: false. The textbook version allocates a buffer proportional to n, the number of items.

lessons.title: Choose, explore and unchoose
lessons.summary: Backtracking walks an implicit decision tree depth first.
lessons.body:
Some problems don't have a clever formula. You simply have to try possibilities: every subset, every ordering, every placement. **Backtracking** is the disciplined way to do that.

Backtracking makes one choice at a time, follows it as far as it can, and when it reaches a dead end it undoes the most recent choice and tries the next option. Marking everything on the current path stops it going round in circles.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: a maze and a piece of chalk
> Walking a maze, at each junction you pick a corridor and chalk a mark on it. At a dead end you walk back to the last junction, rub out the mark and try the next corridor.
>
> **How it maps:** a junction is a decision point; picking a corridor is "choose", walking on is "explore", and walking back and rubbing out the mark is "unchoose". The chalk marks are the shared path state, and trying every corridor in a fixed order makes the search systematic, so no route is missed or repeated.
>
> **Where it stops:** a maze is a fixed physical place. A backtracking search tree usually isn't stored anywhere: the next choices are generated on the fly, the tree can be astronomically large, and the program must also restore any extra bookkeeping (counters, sets of used values), not just the path.

## The state-space tree

Every backtracking problem is a walk over an implicit tree of decisions, its **state-space tree**. Each level is one decision; each edge is one choice; each leaf is a complete candidate.

Generating subsets of `[1, 2, 3]`: at each level decide "include this element or not".

```
                  []
          +1 /         \ skip
          [1]           []
       +2/   \       +2/  \
     [1,2]   [1]    [2]    []
     /  \    / \    / \    / \
 [123][12][13][1][23][2] [3] []
```

The tree has 2³ = 8 leaves, one per subset. Backtracking is a **depth-first** traversal of this tree that builds the current path incrementally and undoes it on the way back.

## The template: choose, explore, unchoose

Almost every backtracking solution has this shape:

```python
def backtrack(state):
    # These helpers are a problem-specific
    # sketch.
    if is_complete(state):
        # Store an independent completed
        # result.
        record(state)
        return
    for choice in choices(state):
        if not is_valid(state, choice):
            continue          # prune
        make(state, choice)   # choose
        backtrack(state)      # explore
        # Restore every mutation before the
        # next choice.
        undo(state, choice)   # unchoose
```

- **Choose** modifies one shared piece of state (append to a path, mark a cell used).
- **Explore** recurses with that choice in place.
- **Unchoose** restores the state *exactly* so that the next choice starts from the same position.

Simple path append/pop updates cost amortised O(1), avoiding a full path copy at each node. Constraint checks and richer updates can cost more; shared mutation alone does not make them constant-time. The abstract helpers in this template are problem-specific.

## Key takeaways
- Backtracking walks an implicit decision tree depth first.
- Undo every mutation so sibling branches begin in exactly the same state.

## Further reading
- [Backtracking — Erickson](https://jeffe.cs.illinois.edu/teaching/algorithms/book/02-backtracking.pdf)
- [Python itertools](https://docs.python.org/3/library/itertools.html)

questions.prompt: In the choose / explore / unchoose template, why does the **unchoose** step exist?

options.text: It removes the solution from the results if it turned out to be invalid
options.explanation: Results are only recorded when a complete, valid solution is reached. Unchoose restores the working search state, not the results list.

options.text: It restores the shared state so the next choice at this level starts from exactly the same position
options.explanation: Correct. The path (and any `used` flags) is shared across the whole search. Undoing the choice means the next sibling branch sees the state as it was before this choice.

options.text: It frees memory used by the recursive call
options.explanation: Returning ends the active call, although frame objects can remain referenced by debuggers or tracebacks. Unchoose is about the shared search state that outlives the call.

options.text: It stops the search once one solution has been found
options.explanation: Stopping early is a separate optimisation (return a flag). Unchoose runs after every explored branch, successful or not.

questions.workedExample:
Consider permutations of [1, 2, 3] with a shared `path` and `used` array.

1. At the root, choose 1: `path = [1]`, `used[0] = True`.
2. Explore everything starting with 1.
3. **Unchoose**: `path = []`, `used[0] = False`.
4. Now choose 2. If we hadn't undone step 1, `path` would be `[1, 2]` and 1 would be marked used, so the branch would be wrong.

Here appending/popping a path entry and changing a used flag cost amortised O(1). More complex state updates or constraint checks may cost more.

lessons.title: Generating subsets without shared-output bugs
lessons.summary: Include/skip and increasing-index loops both enumerate subsets.
lessons.body:
## Subsets

The include/skip version maps directly onto the previous unit’s decision tree:

```python
def subsets(nums):
    res, path = [], []
    def bt(i):
        if i == len(nums):
            res.append(path[:])   # copy!
            return
        path.append(nums[i])      # choose
        bt(i + 1)                 # explore
        path.pop()                # unchoose
        bt(i + 1)                 # skip it
    bt(0)
    return res
```

An equally common version records a subset at **every** node and loops over which element to add next. Starting each loop from `start` ensures each subset is generated once, in one order:

```python
def subsets(nums):
    res, path = [], []
    def bt(start):
        # Store a snapshot, not the shared
        # path.
        res.append(path[:])
        for i in range(start, len(nums)):
            path.append(nums[i])
            bt(i + 1)
            # Restore the path for the next
            # sibling.
            path.pop()
    bt(0)
    return res

# [[], [1], [1,2], [1,2,3], [1,3],
#  [2], [2,3], [3]]
```

Each element is either in or out, independently, so the number of subsets **doubles with every extra element**: 2ⁿ subsets for n distinct elements, counting the empty set and the whole set. Twenty elements give about a million subsets; forty give over a trillion. Copying each finished subset into the result costs up to n steps, so generating them all is O(n·2ⁿ) work.

With forty elements full materialisation is very expensive. Whether it is practical depends on the representation and resources.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: a row of light switches
> A panel of light switches, each on or off, can be set in many patterns. One switch gives 2 patterns, two give 4, three give 8: every switch you add doubles the number of patterns.
>
> **How it maps:** each switch is one element, "on" means the element is in the subset, and each pattern of switches is one subset. The include/skip recursion flips through the patterns one switch at a time, which is why the tree has one level per element and two branches at each node.
>
> **Where it stops:** flipping a switch costs nothing extra. The program also stores each subset as its own list, so every pattern costs memory and copying time proportional to its size.

> [!warning] Append a copy, not the path
> `res.append(path)` stores a reference to the one shared list. After the search finishes, every unchoose has run, `path` is empty, and `res` is a list of identical empty lists: `[[], [], [], []]`. Always append `path[:]` or `list(path)`.

## Key takeaways
- Include/skip and increasing-index loops both enumerate subsets.
- Store a copy of the current path, and count output storage separately from working search state.

## Further reading
- [Backtracking — Erickson](https://jeffe.cs.illinois.edu/teaching/algorithms/book/02-backtracking.pdf)
- [Python itertools](https://docs.python.org/3/library/itertools.html)

options.text: About 1.5 times as long, because the list is 1.5 times longer
options.explanation: That would be linear growth. Subsets come from an independent in/out choice per element, so each extra element doubles the count.

options.text: About a thousand times as long
options.explanation: Correct. Ten extra elements double the number of subsets ten times: 2¹⁰ = 1,024. That uses the stated same-cost-per-subset assumption; in a real run the subsets are also longer on average, so copying them pushes the slowdown higher still.

options.text: About 10 times as long, one step per extra element
options.explanation: That adds work per element instead of multiplying it. Every extra element doubles the whole set of subsets, not adds a fixed amount.

options.text: About 30!/20! times as long, because orderings multiply
options.explanation: Factorials count permutations, where order matters. A subset ignores order, so {1, 2} and {2, 1} are the same subset.

questions.workedExample:
1. The state-space tree has one level per element: include it or skip it.
2. So n elements give 2ⁿ subsets, and every extra element doubles the count.
3. Going from 20 to 30 elements doubles the count ten times: 2¹⁰ = 1,024, about a thousandfold. Twenty elements give about a million subsets; thirty give about a billion.
4. The question assumes the same cost per subset. In a real run each subset is also copied into the result, and the average subset grows from 10 to 15 elements, so the copying alone makes the slowdown nearer fifteen hundred times than a thousand.

That's why subset enumeration only works for small inputs: a few more elements multiply the cost, they don't add to it.

What does this print?

```python

    def bt(i):
        if i == len(nums):
            # This stores the shared
            # list itself.
            res.append(path)
            return

        # Only later indices may follow
        # this one.
        bt(i + 1)
        # Restore the path for the next
        # sibling.
        path.pop()
        # Skip nums[i] and decide the
        # next index.
        bt(i + 1)
    bt(0)
    return res

print(subsets([1, 2]))
```

This assumes the list is frozen at its fullest. But every `append` is matched by a `pop`, so the shared list is empty when the search ends.
Correct. `res` holds four references to the single `path` list. After all the pops, that list is empty, so all four entries print as `[]`.
The base case does append to `res` four times, once per leaf; it's the *contents* of those entries that are wrong.

1. There are 4 leaves, so `res.append(path)` runs 4 times.
2. Each append stores an **object reference** to the same list object, not a snapshot.
3. The search keeps mutating `path`: append 1, append 2, pop, pop, append 2, pop...
4. When `bt(0)` returns, every choice has been undone, so `path == []`.
5. `res` is `[path, path, path, path]`, which prints as `[[], [], [], []]`.

Fix: `res.append(path[:])` (or `list(path)`) to take a copy at the moment the subset is complete.

How does the number of **internal** calls (the calls that branch rather than record a subset) compare, and what does that mean for the total cost?

options.text: About ten times as many internal calls as leaves, because each element adds a level of calls
options.explanation: Each level does add calls, but the upper levels are small: 1, 2, 4, ... calls. They don't each hold as many calls as the bottom level.

options.text: Only about 10 internal calls, one per element
options.explanation: This treats the tree as a single path. Every call at one depth spawns two calls at the next depth, so the levels double.

options.text: One fewer internal call than leaves (1,023), so the total is about twice the number of subsets and still grows like 2ⁿ
options.explanation: Correct. The levels hold 1, 2, 4, ... 512 internal calls, which add up to 1,023, one less than the 1,024 leaves. Total calls are 2,047: about double the output, so the branching adds only a constant factor.

options.text: About 10! internal calls, because the tree branches at every level
options.explanation: 10! counts permutations, whose tree branches by n, n − 1, ... The subset tree branches by exactly 2 at every level.

2. Every level holds one more node than all the levels above it put together. So the 1,023 internal calls are one fewer than the 1,024 leaves.
3. Total calls: 2,047, about twice the number of subsets.

So for n elements the tree has about 2·2ⁿ calls, which is still O(2ⁿ) calls, plus O(n·2ⁿ) for copying the leaves. The exponential output, not the internal bookkeeping, dominates.

lessons.title: Generating permutations
lessons.summary: Track used positions to generate each ordering of distinct values.
lessons.body:
## Permutations

For orderings, every unused element is a possible next choice. A `used` array tracks what's already on the path:

```python
def permutations(nums):
    res, path = [], []
    used = [False] * len(nums)
    def bt():
        if len(path) == len(nums):
            # Store a snapshot, not the
            # shared path.
            res.append(path[:])
            return
        for i, x in enumerate(nums):
            if used[i]:
                continue
            used[i] = True        # choose
            path.append(x)
            bt()                  # explore
            path.pop()            # unchoose
            # Release the position as well
            # as its value.
            used[i] = False
    bt()
    return res

# [1,2,3] -> 123 132 213 231 312 321
```

For n distinct values, the tree has n choices at the root, n − 1 below that, and so on down to 1. Multiplying those choices together gives the number of leaves, **n factorial** (written n!): about 3.6 million orderings for 10 values and over 6 billion for 13. Each finished permutation is copied in up to n steps, so storing them all is O(n·n!) work.

Factorial growth is even steeper than the doubling of subsets: adding one more value multiplies the number of orderings by the new count of values, so going from 10 to 11 values multiplies it by 11.

Repeated input values produce duplicate value sequences unless separately handled.

## Key takeaways
- Track used positions to generate each ordering of distinct values.
- Factorial output growth dominates even with careful working-state bookkeeping.

## Further reading
- [Backtracking — Erickson](https://jeffe.cs.illinois.edu/teaching/algorithms/book/02-backtracking.pdf)
- [Python itertools](https://docs.python.org/3/library/itertools.html)

That's the fifth. The 2-subtree's two permutations must finish before the root moves on to 3.
That's the second, the last permutation in the subtree that starts with 1.
Correct. The order is 123, 132, 213, 231, 312, 321: lexicographic, because the loop tries unused elements left to right at every level.

```

         [2,3,1]  #4
```

options.text: About four times the work, because two more items double the count twice

options.text: About 20% more work, because the items are 20% more numerous
options.explanation: That treats the work as proportional to the number of items. Factorial growth is multiplicative: each added item multiplies the whole count.

options.explanation: Depth affects stack space, not the number of leaves. Each extra level multiplies the leaves by the number of remaining choices.

3. Each stored ordering is also 12 elements instead of 10, so the copying grows by about 132 × 1.2 ≈ 158 times: roughly 5.7 billion element copies.

For n items the work is O(n·n!). These are element-copy counts, not elapsed-time or Python-memory measurements. If you only need to process each permutation, yield it rather than storing it, or prune.

lessons.title: Choosing fixed-size combinations
lessons.summary: A start index prevents reordered copies of the same combination.
lessons.body:
## Combinations

Choosing k items from n without regard to order is subsets with a size limit. Using `start` again prevents `[2, 1]` from appearing after `[1, 2]`:

```python
def combine(n, k):
    if (type(n) is not int or n < 0
            or type(k) is not int or k < 0):
        raise ValueError("nonnegative n, k")
    res, path = [], []
    def bt(start):
        if len(path) == k:
            # Store a snapshot, not the
            # shared path.
            res.append(path[:])
            return
        need = k - len(path)
        # Leave enough later values to
        # finish a result.
        for i in range(start, n - need + 2):
            path.append(i)
            bt(i + 1)
            # Restore the path for the next
            # sibling.
            path.pop()
    bt(1)
    return res

# combine(4, 2) -> [1,2] [1,3] [1,4]
#                  [2,3] [2,4] [3,4]
```

The number of results is the **binomial coefficient**, "n choose k": the number of orderings of all n items, with the orderings inside the chosen group and inside the left-out group divided out, because rearranging them doesn't make a different combination.

```formula reference
C(n, k) = n! / (k! (n − k)!)
where
C(n, k): the number of ways to choose k items from n distinct items when order doesn't matter
n: the number of items to choose from
k: how many items each combination contains, from 0 to n
n!: n factorial, n × (n − 1) × … × 1 (and 0! = 1)
k!: k factorial, the number of orderings of the k chosen items
(n − k)!: the factorial of the number of items left out
In words: count the orderings of all n items, then divide out the orderings inside the chosen group and inside the left-out group, because they don't make a different combination.
```

For four items choosing two, that gives six, matching the six pairs returned by `combine(4, 2)`; the comment shows the result without printing it. The loop bound `n - need + 2` is already a small piece of **pruning**: if you need 2 more numbers, there's no point starting at n.

## Key takeaways
- A start index prevents reordered copies of the same combination.
- The remaining-needed bound avoids branches with too few items left.

## Further reading
- [Backtracking — Erickson](https://jeffe.cs.illinois.edu/teaching/algorithms/book/02-backtracking.pdf)
- [Python itertools](https://docs.python.org/3/library/itertools.html)

Choosing disjoint pairs is not the requirement: each pair is a separate output, and values may recur across outputs.

That is all six unordered pairs from four values: 4 choose 2 is 6.

lessons.title: Pruning combination-sum search
lessons.summary: Reject a partial search state only when its whole subtree is impossible or cannot improve a bound.
lessons.body:
## Pruning: the point of backtracking

Without pruning, backtracking is just brute force with neat bookkeeping. Its real power is abandoning a partial path the moment it can't lead to a valid answer, which skips the **entire subtree** below it.

Two kinds of prune:

- **Feasibility pruning**: the partial solution already breaks a rule (two queens attack each other, the sum exceeds the target).
- **Bound pruning**: the partial solution can't possibly beat the best answer found so far (branch and bound).

### Example: combination sum

Find all combinations of distinct positive integer candidate values (each reusable) that add up to a non-negative integer target. The implementation deduplicates repeated candidate values.

```python
def combination_sum(cands, target):
    cands = list(cands)
    if (type(target) is not int
            or target < 0
            or any(type(c) is not int
                   or c <= 0
                   for c in cands)):
        raise ValueError("candidates")
    # Deduplicate values and permit early
    # stopping.
    cands = sorted(set(cands))
    res, path = [], []
    def bt(start, remaining):
        if remaining == 0:
            # Store a snapshot, not the
            # shared path.
            res.append(path[:])
            return
        for i in range(start, len(cands)):
            c = cands[i]
            if c > remaining:
                break            # prune
            path.append(c)
            # Keep this index available for
            # repeated use.
            bt(i, remaining - c)  # reuse
            # Restore the path for the next
            # sibling.
            path.pop()
    bt(0, target)
    return res

# [2,3,5], 8 -> [2,2,2,2] [2,3,3] [3,5]
```

Sorting first turns a `continue` into a `break`: once one candidate is too big, every later one is too, so the rest of the loop is skipped. Passing `i` (not `i + 1`) allows reuse; restricting the next loop to indices at least i stops `[3, 2, 3]` duplicating `[2, 3, 3]`.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: shopping with a budget
> You have £8 left and a shelf of snacks arranged from cheapest to dearest. As soon as you reach one that costs more than £8, you stop looking along the shelf: everything after it costs even more.
>
> **How it maps:** the money left is `remaining`, the sorted shelf is the sorted list of candidates, and walking away at the first unaffordable item is the `break`. Each skipped item would have started a whole subtree of further choices, so one comparison saves all of them.
>
> **Where it stops:** the shortcut depends on the shelf being sorted and on prices being positive. With unsorted candidates you can only skip one item at a time, and with negative values a later choice could bring the total back down, so the prune would lose answers.

## Complexity at a glance

Here n is the number of input elements and k the size of each combination, with k between zero and n. The earlier enumeration units derived the result counts below; copying each result costs its own length.

| Problem | Results | Time |
|---|---|---|
| Subsets | Exponential | O(n·2ⁿ) |
| Permutations | Factorial | O(n·n!) |
| Size-k combinations | Binomial | O(1 + k·C(n,k)) |
| With pruning | varies | often far less |

For subsets, permutations and combinations, working space is O(n), excluding output. With reusable candidates, the path can be much longer than the number of candidates: the deepest path uses the smallest candidate over and over, so its length is the target divided by the smallest candidate, rounded down. For target 8 with smallest candidate 2 that is [2, 2, 2, 2], four selections deep (plus one frame for the root call).

In general count path, frames and constraint state separately. Counting can omit stored outputs but normally still explores all relevant branches; finding one solution can stop at the first success.

## Key takeaways
- Reject a partial search state only when its whole subtree is impossible or cannot improve a bound.
- Sorted positive candidates allow early break; reuse keeps the same candidate index.

## Further reading
- [Backtracking — Erickson](https://jeffe.cs.illinois.edu/teaching/algorithms/book/02-backtracking.pdf)
- [Python itertools](https://docs.python.org/3/library/itertools.html)

questions.prompt: Combination sum: candidates are a non-empty list of positive integers, sorted ascending; target is non-negative, and each candidate may be reused. Which of these prunes are **safe** (never lose a valid answer)? Select all that apply.

options.text: When a candidate exceeds `remaining`, `break` out of the loop

A prune is safe if the subtree it cuts can't contain a solution.

1. **Break on c > remaining**: sorted order guarantees every later candidate also overshoots. Safe.
2. **Return on remaining < 0**: all values positive, so the sum is monotonic. Safe.
3. **Skip equal-to-previous on the path**: that's a rule for avoiding duplicate *inputs* across siblings, not for reuse along a path. With target 8 it would lose [2, 2, 2, 2]. Unsafe.
4. **Length bound**: safe. Every element is at least the smallest candidate, so a path with more than `target // min(cands)` elements already adds up to more than the target.

lessons.title: Skipping equal sibling choices
lessons.summary: Skip equal values at the same depth, while allowing them at deeper levels.
lessons.body:
The earlier subsets unit recorded a path at every node and recursed only to later indices. Distinct positions are useful for distinct elements, but repeated values make identical result lists. We now keep the increasing-index search while eliminating equal sibling branches.

### Handling duplicate inputs

For `[1, 2, 2]`, the plain subsets code produces `[2]` twice and `[1, 2]` twice. Sort, then skip a value that equals its left neighbour **at the same depth**:

```python
# Equal siblings become adjacent after
# sorting.
nums.sort()
for i in range(start, len(nums)):
    # Skip siblings, not equal values deeper
    # down.
    if i > start and nums[i] == nums[i-1]:
        continue
```

The `i > start` condition is key: it allows `[2, 2]` (the second 2 chosen at a *deeper* level) but forbids starting two sibling branches with equal values. `[1, 2, 2]` then gives 6 distinct subsets instead of 8.

## Key takeaways
- Skip equal values at the same depth, while allowing them at deeper levels.
- A sibling-only test preserves combinations that use repeated values.

## Further reading
- [Backtracking — Erickson](https://jeffe.cs.illinois.edu/teaching/algorithms/book/02-backtracking.pdf)
- [Python itertools](https://docs.python.org/3/library/itertools.html)

This would be the result if *every* repeated 2 were skipped (the `i > 0` bug), losing [2, 2] and [1, 2, 2].
Correct. After sorting to [1, 2, 2]: [], [1], [1,2], [1,2,2], [2], [2,2]. Equal values are skipped only as siblings, so [2, 2] is still reachable.

```
[1]         start=1
[1,2]       i=1
```

lessons.title: Backtracking outside puzzles
lessons.summary: Regex backtracking can explore super-linear or exponential alternatives.
lessons.body:
## Where backtracking shows up

- **Regular expression engines.** Backtracking engines such as Python’s `re` can explore exponentially many alternatives for `(a+)+$` on `"aaaa…ab"`. This can cause **regular-expression denial of service (ReDoS)**. Cloudflare’s 2 July 2019 outage involved a different pattern with super-linear backtracking; it is not evidence that this exact pattern was deployed. RE2 and Rust’s `regex` bound a single search by O(m × n), where m is the size of the regex and n the length of the input, hence linear in the input length for a fixed regex; repeated-search APIs can have different bounds.

> [!note] Measure rejection time separately
> The grouping count explains the growth risk. Seconds depend on the regex engine version, input and machine; measure those explicitly before quoting a runtime.

- **Dependency resolvers.** pip's resolver backtracks: it picks candidate versions and, after a conflict, undoes choices and tries alternative compatible versions; those need not always be older.
- **SAT and constraint solvers** (next lesson), Prolog's execution model, parsers with alternatives, and puzzle solvers.

## Pitfalls

- **Forgetting to unchoose**, or undoing in the wrong order, so later branches start from corrupted state.
- **Appending the shared path** instead of a copy.
- **Generating duplicates** because the loop restarts from 0 instead of `start`.
- **Not pruning early enough**: checking validity only at the leaves turns backtracking back into brute force.
- **Exploding output.** No pruning helps if the answer itself has n! entries.

## Key takeaways
- Regex backtracking can explore super-linear or exponential alternatives.
- Dependency resolution and constraint search undo incompatible choices; their guarantees depend on the actual algorithm.

## Further reading
- [Cloudflare’s 2019 outage](https://blog.cloudflare.com/details-of-the-cloudflare-outage-on-july-2-2019/)
- [pip dependency resolution](https://pip.pypa.io/en/stable/topics/dependency-resolution/)
- [RE2 guarantees](https://github.com/google/re2)

questions.prompt: A web form validates usernames with Python's `re.match(r'(a+)+$', name)`. An attacker submits `'a' * 30 + 'b'`. What happens, and why?

options.text: It fails instantly, because the trailing 'b' doesn't match `$`
options.explanation: A backtracking engine doesn't know the overall match is hopeless. It discovers the failure at 'b' and then retries every other way of splitting the a's between the inner and outer `+`.

options.text: It raises RecursionError after 1,000 levels
options.explanation: Python's `re` engine runs in C with its own backtracking stack; it doesn't hit Python's recursion limit. Its exponential backtracking may consume substantial CPU; an exact duration requires a benchmark.

options.text: It succeeds, matching the first 30 characters
options.explanation: `$` anchors the match at the end of the string, and the 'b' isn't matched by `a+`, so there is no successful match at all.

options.text: It eventually fails after exploring exponentially many possible groupings, potentially consuming substantial CPU time
options.explanation: Correct. Each 'a' can end one inner group or continue it, giving about 2ⁿ splits for n a's, all of which fail at the 'b'. The combinatorial search grows exponentially; elapsed time depends on the interpreter and hardware, so no duration is asserted here.

questions.workedExample:
1. The pattern `(a+)+$` means one or more groups, each of one or more a's, then end of string.
2. Count the ways to divide the a's into groups: each of the 29 gaps between neighbouring a's either is or isn't a group boundary, independently. That is 2 multiplied by itself 29 times: over half a billion groupings.
3. Every division reaches 'b', fails at `$`, and backtracks to try the next division.
4. So the work grows like 2ⁿ for n a's. Exact elapsed time depends on the Python version and machine; no duration is predicted here.
5. This is ReDoS. Fixes: rewrite as `a+$` (equivalent here), cap input length, use a matching library with an enforceable timeout or a separate process that can be killed, or use an engine with an appropriate worst-case search bound. Python’s standard `re` has no timeout argument.

Cloudflare’s 2 July 2019 outage involved a different regex with super-linear backtracking, not this exact exponential pattern.

questions.prompt: Which statements about backtracking are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: Its worst case is usually no better than brute force; its value comes from pruning that skips whole subtrees in practice
options.explanation: Correct. These backtracking searches can have exponential or larger search trees as the instance grows. This is a claim about search algorithms, not that every listed problem inherently requires exponential time; unrestricted N-Queens has direct constructions for one solution.

options.text: With constant-sized frames and path updates, its path/stack memory is O(depth), plus constraint state and stored output
options.explanation: Correct. Only the current path and one frame per level are held at once, unlike BFS, which can hold an entire level.

options.text: It needs the whole state-space tree built in memory before the search starts
options.explanation: The tree is implicit: it's generated on the fly by the loop of choices at each call. That's why backtracking can explore trees with billions of nodes.

options.text: Sorting the choices can turn a per-choice `continue` into a `break` that skips all remaining siblings
options.explanation: Correct. If choices are sorted and one is too large, all later ones are too, so the loop can stop.

options.text: Backtracking always finds an optimal solution faster than a greedy algorithm
options.explanation: Backtracking can *guarantee* optimality by exhaustive search, but it's usually far slower than greedy. When greedy is provably correct, it's the better choice.

questions.workedExample:
Evaluate each:

1. **Worst case comparable to brute force**: true. Pruning can greatly reduce work, but no general polynomial guarantee follows; a problem-specific analysis is needed.
2. **Memory O(depth)**: true. DFS order means one root-to-node path at a time.
3. **Explicit tree**: false. The tree is implicit; the call stack *is* the current path.
4. **Sorted choices → break**: true, as in combination sum.
5. **Faster than greedy**: false. Costs depend on the algorithm and instance. A correct greedy method can be efficient; exhaustive backtracking may be much more expensive.

lessons.title: Modelling N-Queens and attack checks
lessons.summary: One queen per row removes impossible placements before search begins.
lessons.body:
The previous lesson's template enumerates everything. Real backtracking problems are about **search**: the tree is astronomically large, and the craft lies in rejecting bad branches as early and cheaply as possible.

Three ideas do most of the work:

1. **Model the problem well**, so the tree is small to begin with.
2. **Make constraint checks inexpensive**, using incremental bookkeeping where possible.
3. **Propagate consequences** of each choice, so dead ends are spotted before you walk into them.

## N-Queens

Place n queens on an n × n board so that no two share a row, column or diagonal.

### Modelling shrinks the tree

For an eight-by-eight board, compare three ways of framing the search. Each extra piece of structure you build into the model shrinks the number of candidate placements: any 8 of the 64 squares, then exactly one queen per row (8 column choices in each of 8 rows), then one per row and per column (each row takes a different column, so the placements are orderings of the columns).

| Model | Candidates |
|---|---|
| Any 8 of 64 squares | 4,426,165,368 |
| One queen per row | 16,777,216 |
| One per row and column | 40,320 |

Backtracking row by row, rejecting a column the moment it's attacked, makes only **2,057** calls to find all **92** solutions. Each layer of reasoning (rows, then columns, then diagonals checked early) cuts orders of magnitude.

### O(1) attack checks

Every square on the same down-right diagonal has the same `row − col`; every square on the same down-left (anti-) diagonal has the same `row + col`. Moving one step down-right adds 1 to both row and column, so their difference stays the same; moving down-left adds 1 to the row and takes 1 from the column, so their sum stays the same:

```formula reference
r_1 − c_1 = r_2 − c_2
r_1 + c_1 = r_2 + c_2
where
r_1: the row number of the first square, counting from 0 at the top
c_1: the column number of the first square, counting from 0 at the left
r_2: the row number of the second square
c_2: the column number of the second square
In words: two squares share a down-right diagonal exactly when their row-minus-column values match, and share an anti-diagonal exactly when their row-plus-column values match.
```

For example, squares (1, 2) and (3, 0) both have row-plus-column sum 3, so they share an anti-diagonal. Because a diagonal is identified by one number, a set of "used" differences and a set of "used" sums let the solver test both diagonals with two lookups instead of scanning the board.

```
row-col on a 4x4      row+col on a 4x4
  0 -1 -2 -3            0  1  2  3
  1  0 -1 -2            1  2  3  4
  2  1  0 -1            2  3  4  5
  3  2  1  0            3  4  5  6
```

Three sets support expected O(1) lookup per square in the usual hash-table/word-cost model:

```python
def solve_n_queens(n):
    # Reject inputs outside the stated
    # domain.
    if type(n) is not int or n < 0:
        raise ValueError("nonnegative n")
    cols, diag, anti = set(), set(), set()
    queens, out = [], []
    def place(r):
        if r == n:
            out.append(queens[:])
            return
        for c in range(n):
            if (c in cols or r - c in diag
                    or r + c in anti):
                continue          # attacked
            # Register the column and both
            # diagonals.
            cols.add(c)
            diag.add(r - c)
            anti.add(r + c)
            queens.append(c)
            place(r + 1)
            cols.remove(c)
            diag.remove(r - c)
            anti.remove(r + c)
            # Undo every attack marker and
            # this placement.
            queens.pop()
    place(0)
    return out

# n=4 -> [[1, 3, 0, 2], [2, 0, 3, 1]]
```

For board sides four, five, six, seven, eight, ten and twelve respectively, the solution counts are 2, 10, 4, 40, 92, 724 and 14,200.

## Key takeaways
- One queen per row removes impossible placements before search begins.
- Columns and diagonal identities support incremental attack checks and complete undo.

## Further reading
- [N-Queens construction and modelling](https://warwick.ac.uk/fac/sci/maths/general/outreach/urss/n-queens-urss-workbook_16.pdf)

lessons.title: Counting N-Queens with bitmasks
lessons.summary: A mask represents legal columns, and its lowest set bit selects one branch.
lessons.body:
The previous unit placed one queen per row, tracking occupied columns and diagonals. This version counts solutions rather than storing placements. The non-negative integer n is the board side length; a column is one bit in each mask.

### Bitmasks for speed

An alternative uses integer bitmasks instead of sets. Bit i of `cols` means column i is taken. The diagonal masks shift by one each row because a diagonal moves one column per row.

```python
def count_queens(n):
    # Reject inputs outside the stated
    # domain.
    if type(n) is not int or n < 0:
        raise ValueError("nonnegative n")
    # Keep exactly n usable column bits.
    full = (1 << n) - 1
    def go(cols, d1, d2):
        if cols == full:
            return 1
        total = 0
        # Only unattacked board columns
        # remain.
        free = full & ~(cols | d1 | d2)
        while free:
            bit = free & -free   # lowest 1
            # Try each legal column once at
            # this depth.
            free -= bit
            total += go(
                cols | bit,
                ((d1 | bit) << 1) & full,
                (d2 | bit) >> 1)
        return total
    return go(0, 0, 0)
```

`free & -free` isolates the lowest set bit (two's complement trick), so each loop iteration jumps straight to the next legal column. A twelve-by-twelve board has 14,200 solutions. Python integer bit operations scale with the number of machine words needed to hold the masks.

> [!note] Counts are not timings
> A count of 14,200 solutions does not predict execution time. Interpreter, machine, mask width and search strategy affect a benchmark.

> [!note] N-Queens has a direct construction
> For a board side n of one or at least four, direct constructions can place one solution in O(n) output operations without backtracking; board sides two and three have no solution. Backtracking matters when you need all solutions, or for variants with extra constraints.

## Key takeaways
- A mask represents legal columns, and its lowest set bit selects one branch.
- Mask operations and enumeration costs depend on board width and the requested outputs.

## Further reading
- [N-Queens construction and modelling](https://warwick.ac.uk/fac/sci/maths/general/outreach/urss/n-queens-urss-workbook_16.pdf)

questions.prompt: In the bitmask N-Queens solver, `free = 0b101100` (columns 2, 3 and 5 are available). What is `free & -free`, and what does the solver do with it?

options.text: `0b101100`: it tries all free columns at once
options.explanation: `x & -x` keeps just a single bit; it doesn't return `x` unchanged unless x is a power of two.

options.text: `0b100000`: it places a queen in the highest free column
options.explanation: `x & -x` gives the *lowest* set bit. Isolating the highest needs a different operation (e.g. `1 << (x.bit_length() - 1)`).

options.text: `0b000100`: it places a queen in column 2, then clears that bit from `free`
options.explanation: Correct. In two's complement, −x flips all bits above the lowest 1, so the bitwise AND leaves only that bit: column 2.

options.text: `0b000011`: the columns that are not free
options.explanation: Those bits (0 and 1) are the zeros below the lowest 1 in `free`. The bitwise AND with −x keeps the lowest 1 itself, not the zeros.

questions.workedExample:
Work in 8 bits for clarity:

```
 x      = 0010 1100
~x      = 1101 0011
-x = ~x+1 = 1101 0100
x & -x  = 0000 0100
```

So `bit = 0b100`, column 2. The solver then does `free -= bit` (leaving 0b101000) and recurses with that column, diagonal and anti-diagonal blocked. Next iteration picks column 3, then column 5.

lessons.title: Sudoku search with MRV
lessons.summary: Choose the empty cell with the fewest candidates to expose forced moves or failure.
lessons.body:
Unlike queens, Sudoku has one variable per empty cell. We will keep its constraints in row, column and box sets, then search for one completion. Zero marks an empty cell; the displayed solver mutates a list of nine row lists.

## Sudoku

Fill a 9 × 9 grid so each row, column and 3 × 3 box contains 1–9 once. Each empty cell is a **CSP variable** with **CSP domain** {1..9}, and the rules are **CSP constraints** between cells: Sudoku is a textbook **constraint satisfaction problem (CSP)**.

### Plain backtracking

Take the first empty cell, try each digit that doesn't clash with its row, column or box, recurse, undo on failure. It works, but it is blind: it may pick a cell with seven options when another cell has only one.

### Most constrained variable first (MRV)

Choose the empty cell with the **fewest remaining candidates**. Two reasons this helps:

- A cell with one candidate is a forced move: no branching at all.
- A cell with zero candidates proves the current branch is dead, immediately.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: a wedding seating plan
> When seating guests, you place the awkward ones first: the guest who can only sit at one table because of who they must avoid, before the easy-going guest who is happy anywhere. If someone turns out to have no acceptable table at all, you find out straight away instead of after seating everyone else.
>
> **How it maps:** guests are empty cells, acceptable tables are each cell's candidate digits, and "awkward guest first" is MRV: branch on the variable with the fewest remaining values. A guest with one option is a forced move; a guest with none is an early dead end.
>
> **Where it stops:** the person doing the seating plan can rearrange the whole room at the end. The solver commits cell by cell and must undo assignments in reverse order when a branch fails, and recomputing every cell's candidates to find the smallest set has its own cost on each step.

```python
def solve(grid):
    if (len(grid) != 9
            or any(len(row) != 9
                   for row in grid)):
        raise ValueError("expected 9 by 9")
    if any(type(d) is not int
           or not 0 <= d <= 9
           for row in grid for d in row):
        raise ValueError("digits 0..9")
    rows = [set() for _ in range(9)]
    cols = [set() for _ in range(9)]
    boxes = [set() for _ in range(9)]
    empty = []
    for r in range(9):
        for c in range(9):
            if d := grid[r][c]:
                b = r//3*3 + c//3
                if (d in rows[r]
                        or d in cols[c]
                        or d in boxes[b]):
                    return False
                rows[r].add(d)
                cols[c].add(d)
                boxes[r//3*3 + c//3].add(d)
            else:
                # Record empty cells for
                # variable selection.
                empty.append((r, c))

    def cands(r, c):
        b = r//3*3 + c//3
        # Any unit can exclude a candidate
        # digit.
        used = rows[r] | cols[c] | boxes[b]
        return [d for d in range(1, 10)
                if d not in used]

    def bt():
        if not empty:
            return True
        i = min(range(len(empty)),
                key=lambda i:
                    len(cands(*empty[i])))
        # Remove the most constrained empty
        # cell.
        r, c = empty.pop(i)
        b = r//3*3 + c//3
        for d in cands(r, c):
            grid[r][c] = d
            rows[r].add(d)
            cols[c].add(d)
            boxes[b].add(d)
            # Return on the first complete
            # solution.
            if bt():
                return True
            rows[r].remove(d)
            cols[c].remove(d)
            boxes[b].remove(d)
        grid[r][c] = 0
        # Restore this cell at its former
        # position.
        empty.insert(i, (r, c))
        return False

    return bt()
```

> [!note] Heuristics depend on the puzzle
> MRV can reduce search, but its improvement is instance-dependent. Compare an exact puzzle and baseline solver with the same call-counting convention before drawing a numerical conclusion.

## Key takeaways
- Choose the empty cell with the fewest candidates to expose forced moves or failure.
- Restore grid, unit sets and the empty-cell list together when a branch fails.

## Further reading
- [Peter Norvig: Solving Every Sudoku Puzzle](https://norvig.com/sudoku.html)

lessons.title: Propagation, exact cover and SAT
lessons.summary: Naked and hidden singles eliminate candidates before guessing.
lessons.body:
The previous Sudoku unit chose the cell with the smallest candidate set. Propagation removes impossible values and makes forced assignments before branching. The examples below distinguish these deductions from variable ordering and explain how wider solver frameworks encode constraints.

### Constraint propagation

MRV picks good cells; **propagation** goes further by deducing values before guessing. Peter Norvig's well-known solver keeps a set of possible digits for every cell and applies two rules repeatedly:

1. **Naked single**: if a cell has only one possible digit, assign it and remove that digit from all its 20 peers.
2. **Hidden single**: if a digit has only one possible cell in a row, column or box, it must go there.

Each assignment can trigger more eliminations, which trigger more assignments. Many easy puzzles are solved by propagation alone, with no search at all. When propagation stalls, the solver picks the MRV cell, guesses, propagates again, and backtracks if any cell's set becomes empty.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: filling in a crossword
> Writing in one answer fixes letters in every answer that crosses it. Those letters often leave only one possible word for a crossing clue, which fixes more letters, and so on. You only start guessing when no clue is forced any more.
>
> **How it maps:** each crossword entry is a variable, the dictionary words that still fit are its domain, and crossing squares are constraints. Writing in an answer and updating the crossing entries is propagation; an entry with exactly one fitting word is a naked single.
>
> **Where it stops:** a person solving a crossword can rub out answers in any order. A propagating solver must record every elimination it made after a guess so it can restore exactly those candidates when the guess fails.

## Constraint propagation in general

All of this generalises to CSPs: variables, domains and constraints. Solvers combine backtracking with:

| Technique | Idea |
|---|---|
| MRV | Branch on the smallest domain |
| Degree heuristic | Tie-break by most constraints |
| Least constraining value | Try values that leave neighbours most options |
| Forward checking | After assigning, prune neighbours' domains; fail if one empties |
| Arc consistency (AC-3) | For binary constraints, retain a value only if it has support in each constrained neighbour |

**Forward checking** looks one step ahead. **Arc consistency** propagates further: removing a value from one domain can remove values from others, and so on, until nothing changes. Propagation has a per-node cost and can reduce the search tree; whether it improves running time depends on the instance and implementation.

**Exact cover** is the problem of choosing rows of a 0/1 table so that every column has exactly one 1 among the chosen rows. Sudoku fits it directly: each row of the table is one possible (cell, digit) placement, 81 cells times 9 digits = 729 rows, and each column is one rule that must be satisfied exactly once. There are four kinds of rule with 81 of each: every cell is filled, and every digit appears once in every row, once in every column and once in every box, giving 324 columns before the givens remove candidates.

Knuth’s **Algorithm X** can be implemented with **dancing links** (DLX): restoring an individual removed link/node takes O(1), while undoing a whole choice may restore many nodes. N-Queens uses exactly-one row/column constraints and **at-most-one diagonal** constraints, so the direct formulation needs optional secondary columns (generalised exact cover) or another encoding.

**SAT solvers.** The DPLL algorithm is backtracking plus **unit propagation** (an unsatisfied clause with one unassigned literal and all others false forces it). Modern CDCL solvers add clause learning and non-chronological backjumping, and can solve substantial structured instances; size alone does not determine difficulty. They power hardware verification, scheduling and package managers: libsolv (used by DNF and by conda's libmamba solver) resolves dependencies with SAT techniques, while pip's resolver backtracks over candidate versions.

## Key takeaways
- Naked and hidden singles eliminate candidates before guessing.
- Forward checking, arc consistency, exact cover and SAT organise constraints differently.

## Further reading
- [Peter Norvig: Solving Every Sudoku Puzzle](https://norvig.com/sudoku.html)
- [Knuth: Dancing Links](https://arxiv.org/pdf/cs/0011047)
- [CSP ordering and propagation — Berkeley notes](https://berkeleyai.github.io/cs188-website/assets/notes/n2.pdf)

questions.prompt: Which statements about CSP search heuristics are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: MRV (fewest remaining values) tends to find dead ends early, because a variable with an empty domain is picked immediately
options.explanation: Correct. If any variable has zero options, MRV selects it first and the branch fails at once instead of after more guessing.

options.text: Least-constraining-value orders the *values* of the chosen variable so that neighbours keep as many options as possible
options.explanation: Correct. MRV chooses *which variable*; LCV chooses *which value to try first*, aiming to succeed without backtracking.

options.text: Forward checking removes neighbour values inconsistent with the new assignment and backtracks if any domain becomes empty
options.explanation: Correct. It's one step of lookahead, catching some failures before recursing.

options.text: Arc consistency is weaker than forward checking because it only looks at one constraint at a time
options.explanation: Backwards. For the same binary constraints and domains, AC-3 revises arcs until nothing changes and prunes at least what forward checking would remove after that assignment.

options.text: Heuristics like MRV change which solutions exist
options.explanation: They only change the *order* of the search. The solution set is fixed by the constraints.

| LCV | which value first |

options.text: Nothing until X's candidates shrink to one

2. For digit 7 in this row, the possible cells are {X}.
3. So 7 must go in X. This is a **hidden single**: the cell has several candidates, but the digit has only one home in this unit.
4. Put digit 7 in cell X, remove 7 from X's column and box peers, and remove 3 and 9 from consideration for X.

options.text: DPLL is backtracking over Boolean variables plus unit propagation: an unsatisfied clause with one unassigned literal and all others false forces that literal
options.explanation: Correct. Unit propagation is SAT's equivalent of a naked single.

options.text: Knuth's Algorithm X with dancing links restores an individual removed node in constant time; undoing a whole choice may restore many nodes
options.explanation: Correct. Removed nodes keep their own links, so reinserting them is O(1) per node; that's the 'dance'.

options.text: Sudoku as exact cover has 729 potential rows (cell × digit) and 324 constraint columns before givens eliminate candidates
options.explanation: Correct. 81 cells, 81 row-digit, 81 column-digit and 81 box-digit constraints = 324, each covered exactly once.

options.explanation: Generalised n² × n² Sudoku is NP-complete. Propagation alone is not guaranteed to decide every instance; NP-completeness does not by itself prove that every solving method must search or that P ≠ NP.

options.explanation: Conventional CDCL uses learned clauses and can backjump non-chronologically, undoing multiple decisions; some modern variants also use chronological backtracking.

questions.workedExample:
1. **DPLL**: true. Branch on a variable, propagate unit clauses, backtrack after a conflict.
2. **DLX**: true. Removing node x does `x.left.right = x.right` and `x.right.left = x.left`; x still remembers its neighbours, so restoring is two pointer writes.
3. **Exact cover sizes**: 9 × 9 × 9 = 729 candidates; 4 × 81 = 324 constraints. True.
4. **Polynomial guarantee**: false; the general problem is NP-complete.
5. **Chronological CDCL**: false; conventional CDCL can backjump non-chronologically, although variants also exist.

lessons.title: Word search with reversible marking
lessons.summary: Mark the current path without losing original letters, then restore on both success and failure.
lessons.body:
## Word search

Given a rectangular grid of single-character strings, is a word spelled by a path of horizontally or vertically adjacent cells, using each cell no more than once? The empty word is accepted; a non-empty word on an empty board is rejected.

```python
def exist(board, word):
    if not word:
        return True
    if not board or not board[0]:
        return False
    R, C = len(board), len(board[0])
    if any(len(row) != C for row in board):
        raise ValueError("ragged board")
    if len(word) > R * C:
        return False
    # A unique object cannot match a word
    # letter.
    used = object()  # cannot equal a letter
    def dfs(r, c, k):
        if k == len(word):
            return True
        if not (0 <= r < R and 0 <= c < C):
            return False
        if board[r][c] != word[k]:
            return False
        ch, board[r][c] = board[r][c], used
        found = (dfs(r+1, c, k+1) or
                 dfs(r-1, c, k+1) or
                 dfs(r, c+1, k+1) or
                 dfs(r, c-1, k+1))
        # Restore on failure and on success
        # alike.
        board[r][c] = ch          # restore
        return found
    return any(dfs(r, c, 0)
               for r in range(R)
               for c in range(C))
```

- **Choose** = temporarily replace the cell with a unique object, which cannot equal a string character. This avoids a separate visited set; relative speed requires measurement.
- **Unchoose** = restore the letter. Forget this and a failed path permanently blocks cells that a later path needs.
- **Prune** = the letter mismatch check, which can reject a branch immediately; its effectiveness depends on the grid and word.

Complexity: count the paths the search can try. Every cell is a possible start; the first step has 4 directions and every later step at most 3, because the cell you came from is already on the path. So every extra letter in the word can multiply the number of paths by up to 3.

```formula reference
P ≤ 4RC 3^{L − 2}
where
P: the number of paths the search may explore, an upper bound
R: the number of rows in the grid
C: the number of columns in the grid
L: the length of the word, in letters (at least 2)
3^{L − 2}: L − 2 copies of 3 multiplied together
≤: at most
In words: every cell can start a path, the first step has up to 4 directions and each later step at most 3; a 3 × 4 grid and a 10-letter word allow at most about 315,000 paths.
```

So for an R-row, C-column grid the worst case is **O(R·C·3ᴸ)** for a word of length L. Mismatches and boundaries can reduce this upper bound, but no reduction is guaranteed for every input.

## Key takeaways
- Mark the current path without losing original letters, then restore on both success and failure.
- The branching bound is an upper bound; boundaries and mismatches can reduce actual work.

## Further reading
- [Backtracking — Erickson](https://jeffe.cs.illinois.edu/teaching/algorithms/book/02-backtracking.pdf)

questions.prompt: In the word search DFS, why does the code overwrite the current cell with a unique marker object before exploring its neighbours?

options.text: To mark the cell as part of a found word in the final output
options.explanation: The grid is restored after each attempt; the marker is temporary bookkeeping, not output.

options.text: To stop the path from using the same cell twice
options.explanation: Correct. A neighbour's DFS will see the marker, which never matches a letter, so the current path can't loop back through this cell.

options.text: To speed up the letter comparison
options.explanation: The comparison costs the same either way. the marker exists to block reuse, which the problem rules forbid.

options.text: To prevent other starting cells from ever visiting it
options.explanation: The cell is restored when this DFS call returns, so other paths and starting cells can use it. Only the *current* path is blocked.

questions.workedExample:
1. The rules say each cell may be used no more than once per word.
2. Without marking, searching for a word spelled A, B, A could go A → B → back to the same A.
3. Writing the marker makes the cell fail the `board[r][c] != word[k]` check for the rest of this path. It's a visited set stored in the grid itself, without a separate visited set; the recursion still stores state.
4. Restoring the letter afterwards (unchoose) frees the cell for other paths.

questions.prompt:
A version of word search forgets to restore the cell (it sets `board[r][c] = "#"` but never puts the letter back). Grid and query:

```
A A B
A B A
```

`exist(board, "AAA")` is called, scanning start cells row by row. What does the buggy version return, versus the correct version?

options.text: Buggy returns False; correct returns True
options.explanation: Correct. The first start (0,0) explores (1,0) and (0,1), fails, and leaves all three as `#`. Every later start then finds those cells blocked.

options.text: Both return True
options.explanation: The correct version does, via (0,1) → (0,0) → (1,0). But the buggy version's first failed attempts leave `#` behind on exactly those cells.

options.text: Both return False, because no three A's are in a line
options.explanation: The path doesn't need to be straight: (0,1) → (0,0) → (1,0) turns a corner, which is allowed.

options.text: Buggy raises an IndexError
options.explanation: Bounds are still checked before indexing; the bug corrupts the grid's contents, not its shape.

questions.workedExample:
1. Correct version: start (0,0): down to (1,0), then no unvisited A neighbour; right to (0,1), then no A neighbour except (0,0), which is on the path. Fail, restore. Start (0,1): left to (0,0), down to (1,0) → "AAA". **True**.
2. Buggy version, start (0,0): marks (0,0), tries (1,0) (marks it), fails; tries (0,1) (marks it), fails.
3. Now (0,0), (1,0) and (0,1) are all `#` permanently.
4. Remaining A's: (1,2) only. Its neighbours are B, B and out of bounds. **False**.

Lesson: every choose must have a matching unchoose, even on failure paths.

questions.prompt: On a fixed grid, ignoring letters entirely, a word-search DFS has a coarse worst-case bound on the paths it may explore: every cell can start a path, the first step has up to 4 directions and each later step at most 3. The word you search for grows from 6 letters to **8** letters. How does that worst-case bound change?

options.text: It grows by a third, because the word is a third longer
options.explanation: That treats the work as linear in the word length. Each extra letter is an extra branching step, which multiplies the paths.

options.text: It grows by a factor of 16, four directions per extra letter
options.explanation: Four directions are available only at the first step. After that, the cell you came from is on the path, leaving at most 3.

options.text: It stays the same, because the number of starting cells is unchanged
options.explanation: The starting cells fix only the first factor. Each later letter adds another step with up to 3 branches.

options.text: It grows by a factor of up to 9: two more steps of at most 3 branches each
options.explanation: Correct. Two extra letters add two more moves, each with at most 3 new directions, so the bound multiplies by 3 × 3 = 9. Letter mismatches and edges usually cut the real count far below the bound.

questions.workedExample:
1. A path for an L-letter word visits L cells: a start cell, then L − 1 moves.
2. The first move has up to 4 directions; every later move has at most 3, because one neighbour is the cell you just came from (and is marked as used).
3. Lengthening the word from 6 to 8 letters adds two later moves, each multiplying the bound by at most 3: a factor of **9**. (On a 4 × 4 grid the bound rises from 5,184 to 46,656 paths.)

That is why the worst case is O(R·C·3ᴸ) for an R × C grid: exponential in the word length, linear in the grid size. Letter mismatches and grid boundaries can reduce the explored count; that reduction is input-dependent.

lessons.title: Many-word search and solver pitfalls
lessons.summary: A trie shares prefix work across dictionary words.
lessons.body:
The previous word-search unit used reversible marking for one word. A dictionary introduces shared prefixes: different target words may begin along exactly the same grid path. We can reuse that search while preserving the rule that a cell appears only once on the current path.

### Many words at once

To find which of thousands of words appear in the grid, don't run `exist` per word. Put all words in a **trie** and do one DFS from each cell that walks the grid and the trie together. You stop as soon as the current path isn't a prefix of any word, and you clear a found word’s terminal marker and optionally delete exhausted branches, preserving nodes still needed by longer words.

## Pitfalls

- **Expensive validity checks.** Scanning units costs their length; fixed 9 × 9 Sudoku has constant-size units. Incremental sets give expected constant-time membership, and bitmask cost depends on the represented width.
- **Incomplete undo.** Every structure updated in "choose" (grid, sets, masks, the empty list) must be restored in "unchoose".
- **Continuing after success.** If you need one solution, propagate a `True` back up and stop.
- **Symmetry.** N-Queens solutions come in groups of up to 8 under rotation and reflection (8-Queens has 12 fundamentally different solutions). Breaking symmetry, for example searching mirrored first-row branches only once, can reduce work. For odd n, handle the centre column separately; enumerating all solutions requires restoring omitted symmetric solutions.

## Key takeaways
- A trie shares prefix work across dictionary words.
- Undo, success propagation and symmetry handling must match whether one or all solutions are requested.

## Further reading
- [Backtracking — Erickson](https://jeffe.cs.illinois.edu/teaching/algorithms/book/02-backtracking.pdf)
- [Knuth: Dancing Links](https://arxiv.org/pdf/cs/0011047)

questions.prompt: You must find which of 50,000 dictionary words appear in a 12 × 12 letter grid (word-search rules). Running the single-word `exist` for each word is too slow. What's the best approach?

options.text: Sort the words and binary-search the grid for each one
options.explanation: A grid isn't an ordered sequence, so binary search doesn't apply. Each word still needs its own DFS.

options.text: Build a trie of all words, then DFS once from each cell, walking the trie alongside the path and stopping when the prefix isn't in the trie
options.explanation: Correct. Shared prefixes are explored once, and any path whose prefix matches no word is cut immediately. Removing found words from the trie prunes further.

options.text: Enumerate every path in the grid up to the longest word length and look each up in a hash set
options.explanation: For a 12 by 12 grid, 144 start cells and a word length L, even the coarse O(144 × 3ᴸ) path bound is large. For ten letters its scale expression is about 8.5 million, not a measured path count. Without prefix pruning many explored paths may be irrelevant.

options.text: Run the 50,000 searches in parallel threads
options.explanation: Threads do not guarantee division of running time by core count or remove repeated work. In a GIL-enabled CPython build, CPU-bound Python bytecode does not execute concurrently across threads; free-threaded builds differ.

questions.workedExample:
1. Per-word DFS repeats work: "STAR", "START" and "STARE" all re-explore the same S → T → A → R paths.
2. A trie merges common prefixes into one path of nodes.
3. DFS from each cell, moving to child `trie[ch]` at each step. If `ch` isn't a child, stop: no word starts with this path.
4. When a node marks the end of a word, record it and clear its terminal marker (pruning only branches no longer needed by another word) so it isn't found again.
5. The search now costs roughly the number of grid paths that are prefixes of real words, which can be much smaller than all paths, depending on the dictionary and grid.

lessons.title: Greedy choice and interval scheduling
lessons.summary: A locally attractive choice needs a proof of safety.
lessons.body:
Backtracking tries every option and undoes bad ones. A **greedy algorithm** does the opposite: at each step it makes the choice that looks best *right now*, commits to it, and never reconsiders.

That makes greedy algorithms fast (often just a sort and a single pass) and simple to write. The catch is that "looks best right now" is frequently wrong. The hard part of greedy isn't the code; it's knowing whether the greedy choice is **safe**, and proving it.

## The two properties

A greedy algorithm produces an optimal answer when the problem has:

1. **The greedy choice property**: some optimal solution begins with the greedy choice. Making it never rules out the best answer.
2. **Optimal substructure**: after making the choice, what remains is a smaller instance of the same problem, and an optimal solution to it combines with the choice to give an optimal whole.

Optimal substructure is shared with dynamic programming. The greedy choice property is what lets greedy skip DP's "try every option and take the best": one option is provably enough.

## Interval scheduling

You have one meeting room and a list of requested meetings `(start, end)`. In both interval examples assume finite real endpoints with start < end, representing positive-duration **half-open intervals** [start, end): each meeting includes its start time but not its end time, so a meeting ending at 10 doesn't clash with one starting at 10. Accept as **many** meetings as possible with no overlaps. (In CLRS this is the **activity selection** problem.)

Several greedy rules sound plausible:

| Rule | Works? |
|---|---|
| Earliest start first | No |
| Shortest meeting first | No |
| Fewest conflicts first | No |
| **Earliest finish first** | **Yes** |

Counterexamples kill the wrong rules quickly:

```
Earliest start fails:
  [0-----------------10]
    [1-2] [3-4] [5-6]
  picks 1 meeting; best is 3

Shortest first fails:
  [1-----5]    [6-----10]
        [4--7]
  picks [4,7] alone; best is 2
```

The winning rule: **sort by end time, and take each meeting that starts at or after the last accepted one ends.**

```python
def max_meetings(intervals):
    chosen = []
    last_end = float("-inf")
    by_end = sorted(intervals,
                    key=lambda iv: iv[1])
    for s, e in by_end:
        # Half-open meetings may touch
        # endpoints.
        if s >= last_end:   # compatible
            chosen.append((s, e))
            # Only an accepted meeting
            # changes the boundary.
            last_end = e
    return chosen
```

For n meetings, the sort dominates: **O(n log n)**, and the loop afterwards is a single O(n) pass. The `>=` treats a meeting ending at 10 and one starting at 10 as compatible; use `>` if touching intervals conflict in your problem.

> [!example] Trace
> Meetings sorted by end: (1,4), (3,5), (0,6), (5,7), (3,9), (5,9), (6,10), (8,11), (8,12), (2,14), (12,16).
> - Take (1,4). last_end = 4.
> - (3,5), (0,6) start before 4: skip. Take (5,7). last_end = 7.
> - (3,9), (5,9), (6,10) start before 7: skip. Take (8,11). last_end = 11.
> - (8,12), (2,14) start before 11: skip. Take (12,16).
>
> Result: 4 meetings.

## Key takeaways
- A locally attractive choice needs a proof of safety.
- For maximum meeting count, sort by finish time and accept compatible half-open intervals.

## Further reading
- [Greedy algorithms and Huffman codes — Erickson](https://jeffe.cs.illinois.edu/teaching/algorithms/book/04-greedy.pdf)
- [Python heapq](https://docs.python.org/3/library/heapq.html)

lessons.title: Proving earliest-finish greedy
lessons.summary: Swap the earliest-finishing meeting into an optimal solution without losing later meetings.
lessons.body:
The previous unit schedules positive-duration half-open intervals by earliest finish time. This unit proves that this rule maximises the number accepted; it does not yet assert any guarantee about meetings with different values.

### Why it's correct: the exchange argument

The standard proof technique for greedy is the **exchange argument**: take any optimal solution, and show you can swap in the greedy choice without making it worse.

1. Let g be the meeting with the earliest finish time overall.
2. Take any optimal schedule O, and let o be its first meeting.
3. Since g finishes earliest of all, it ends no later than o.
4. Replace o with g. Every other meeting in O starts at or after the end of o, which is at or after the end of g, so none of them overlap g:

```formula reference
e_g ≤ e_o ≤ s_x
where
e_g: the end time of g, the meeting that finishes first overall
e_o: the end time of o, the first meeting in the optimal schedule O
s_x: the start time of any other meeting x in O
≤: is at or before (less than or equal to)
In words: g ends no later than o, and every later meeting in O starts no earlier than o ends, so swapping o for g creates no clash.
```

5. The new schedule is still valid and has the same size: it's also optimal, and it starts with g.

So the greedy first choice is safe (greedy choice property). After choosing g, the remaining problem is "schedule the meetings starting at or after the end of g", the same problem on a smaller input (optimal substructure). Induction finishes the proof.

A related proof style is **greedy stays ahead**: show that after k steps, greedy's k-th meeting ends no later than the k-th meeting of any other valid schedule. Then greedy can never fall behind, so it fits at least as many.

## Key takeaways
- Swap the earliest-finishing meeting into an optimal solution without losing later meetings.
- The remaining compatible meetings form the same problem, so induction completes the proof.

## Further reading
- [Greedy correctness — Erickson](https://jeffe.cs.illinois.edu/teaching/algorithms/book/04-greedy.pdf)

questions.prompt: An exchange proof for earliest-finish-first uses a greedy meeting g and an optimal schedule O whose first meeting o differs from g. Which statement justifies replacing o with g while preserving validity and the number of meetings?

options.text: Since g is shorter than o, g fits wherever o did
options.explanation: Earliest finish doesn't mean shortest: g might be longer than o and start earlier. The proof relies on *end* times, not lengths.

options.text: g ends no later than o, and all other meetings in O start at or after o ends
options.explanation: Correct. g ends no later than o, so anything that was compatible with o (by starting after o ended) is also compatible with g.

options.text: g starts no later than o, so g comes first in any schedule
options.explanation: Start times aren't what matter; g could start before o and still overlap nothing in O − {o}, but the reason is its early end.

options.text: Since greedy chose g, it must be in every optimal schedule
options.explanation: That's circular, and false: optimal schedules needn't contain g. The argument only shows *some* optimal schedule does.

questions.workedExample:
The structure of an exchange argument:

1. Take an arbitrary optimal solution O.
2. If it already agrees with greedy's first choice, done.
3. Otherwise, modify it to include the greedy choice and show it stays valid and no worse.

Here, O's intervals after o all start at or after o ends (O is valid and o is first), and g ends no later than o because g finishes earliest of *all* intervals. So every other interval in O also starts at or after g ends.

Swap o out and g in. The new schedule has no clashes and exactly as many meetings as O, so it is valid, the same size, and therefore also optimal. Then induct on the subproblem of intervals starting at or after the end of g.
